summary: Follow-up plan for stage GN.4 (Lattice points and homogeneous dynamics) of the geometry-of-numbers roadmap. It cites the base packet's 46 GN.4 nodes and the GN.1 follow-up's four Gaussian covering nodes and plans what their coverage records and the routed papers and consumer requests leave open. Counting: volumes of coordinate projections and Davenport's principle, semialgebraic sets of bounded complexity with a uniform interval condition from a fibrewise cell count, Davenport's estimate for triangular unipotent images (with the reorganised induction its source omits), ball counts by successive minima derived from Henk's bound, Schmidt's bounded-domain count, counts for definite quadratic lattices, small-vector counts, bases with coordinate bounds, Widmer's lattice-uniform count for Lipschitz boundaries and Barroero–Widmer's count for semialgebraic families; Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin's angular bands, primitive lattices with prescribed minima, Schmidt's extension count, band section volumes, weighted primitive sums and primitive ball counts; Bhargava–Shankar–Wang's skew counts of singular symmetric matrices through Eskin–Katznelson row lattices; curvature-controlled planar counts after van der Corput and Huxley; Markoff fundamental-set counts; Blomer–Granville; lattice points on a hyperplane in the orthant. Transference and covering: Minkowski-constant transference, sup-norm covering from the dual lattice, the minimum of a Construction A lattice. Dynamics: the space of unimodular lattices and its invariant probability, Mahler's criterion with bounded bases and the sup norm, diagonal and unipotent flows, the Mautner phenomenon, mixing of noncompact one-parameter flows and of the time-one diagonal map on X_2, good functions and Kleinbock–Margulis quantitative nondivergence with its unipotent corollary, Borel density and the auxiliary lemmas of Margulis's proof of the Oppenheim conjecture. Siegel: the Siegel transform, mirabolic unfolding, invariant measures on the punctured space and the primitive mean value theorem. Equidistribution carriers: CM point packets, oriented closed geodesics with their length and orientation reversal, harmonic Weyl sums and the spherical Weyl criterion; the equidistribution theorems on the modular surface are proposed for the toral-packets Part II because their inputs lie above this tier.

sourceIssues.printed: The proposition asserts the lattice-point estimate for images R′ = uR of a bounded semialgebraic multiset under triangular unipotent u, with the error measured by projection volumes of R rather than of R′, and says Davenport's proof adapts without significant change.
sourceIssues.correction: Davenport's slicing argument applied to R′ produces projection volumes of R′, which can be much larger than those of R (a shear stretches the first-coordinate projection). nodes.title: Volumes of coordinate projections
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1 and Z ⊆ ℝⁿ (ℝⁿ = Fin n → ℝ with Lebesgue measure). For J ⊆ Fin n let π_J : ℝⁿ → ℝ^J be the coordinate projection and V_J(Z) = vol_J(π_J(Z)) ∈ [0, ∞] its outer Lebesgue measure on ℝ^J. For 0 ≤ j ≤ n put V_j(Z) = Σ_{|J| = j} V_J(Z), with the convention V_0(Z) = 1, so V_n(Z) = vol(Z). The projection maximum of Bhargava–Shankar is Vol(Z̄) = max{V_J(Z) : 1 ≤ |J| ≤ n − 1}, which is 0 when n = 1.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; Z arbitrary (outer measure, so no measurability is assumed). V_0 = 1 is a convention for the constant term of the error, not the measure of a point; it is used even for Z = ∅ only inside error bounds, which are then trivially true.
proofSteps: V_J is the composite of the image under the measurable linear map π_J with the outer measure on ℝ^J; V_{Fin n} = vol because π_{Fin n} is the identity up to the canonical equivalence ℝⁿ ≃ ℝ^{Fin n}.
Monotonicity, translation invariance and the scaling law |c|^{|J|} follow from the same properties of Lebesgue measure on ℝ^J and from π_J(c·Z + v) = c·π_J(Z) + π_J(v).

For an upper triangular unipotent u (u_ii = 1, u_ij = 0 for i > j) and a final segment J = {k, …, n − 1}, π_J ∘ u = u_J ∘ π_J with u_J the unipotent lower-right block, so V_J(uZ) = V_J(Z); for other J this fails (test proj_volume_shear).
acceptance: The unit cube has V_J = 1 for every J and V_j = C(n, j).
For the box [0, a] × [0, b] ⊂ ℝ²: V_1 = a + b, V_2 = ab.

nodes.title: Davenport's principle for coordinate-convex regions
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, h ≥ 1 and Z ⊆ ℝⁿ compact. Suppose (1) every line parallel to a coordinate axis meets Z in the empty set or a union of at most h closed intervals (single points allowed), and (2) for every J ⊆ Fin n with 1 ≤ |J| ≤ n − 1 the projection π_J(Z) ⊆ ℝ^J has the same property for lines parallel to the axes of ℝ^J. Then |#(Z ∩ ℤⁿ) − vol(Z)| ≤ Σ_{j=0}^{n−1} h^{n−j} V_j(Z), with V_j as in coordinate-projection-volumes (V_0 = 1).
hypotheses: Compactness makes every projection compact, hence measurable, and every interval of a line section closed.
The constant is explicit; no uniformity in a family is claimed here (that is semialgebraic-interval-condition).
proofSteps: n = 1: Z is a union of at most h closed intervals I and |#(I ∩ ℤ) − len I| ≤ 1 for each.

n > 1: write N(Z) = Σ_{t∈ℤ} N(Z^{(t)}) over the slices Z^{(t)} = {y ∈ ℝ^{n−1} : (t, y) ∈ Z}. Each slice satisfies (1)–(2) in dimension n − 1, since the projections of a slice are slices of projections of Z and lines in a slice are lines in ℝⁿ; apply the induction hypothesis.

Main term: by Tonelli, Σ_{t∈ℤ} vol_{n−1}(Z^{(t)}) = ∫_{ℝ^{n−1}} #{t ∈ ℤ : (t, y) ∈ Z} dy, and the integrand differs from the length of the fibre over y by at most h, so the sum is vol(Z) + O(h·V_{n−1}-term of the projection forgetting the first coordinate).

Error terms: Σ_t V_J(Z^{(t)}) for J ⊆ {2, …, n} is again a lattice sum of slice volumes of π_{{1}∪J}(Z), estimated by the same Tonelli step; collecting the powers of h gives the stated bound (Davenport's induction, as reproduced by Barroero–Widmer).
acceptance: Z = [0, N]ⁿ with N ∈ ℕ: #(Z ∩ ℤⁿ) − vol Z = (N+1)ⁿ − Nⁿ ≤ Σ_{j<n} C(n,j) N^j, the bound with h = 1.
A finite set of h points on the x-axis in ℝ¹ has volume 0 and at most h lattice points: the bound h·V_0 = h is attained.

nodes.title: Semialgebraic sets and multisets of bounded complexity
nodes.statement: Let n, k, ℓ ∈ ℕ. A set S ⊆ ℝⁿ has description complexity at most (k, ℓ) if there are polynomials f_1, …, f_k ∈ ℝ[x_1, …, x_n] of total degree ≤ ℓ and a set Σ ⊆ {−1, 0, 1}^k of sign vectors with S = {x : (sign f_1(x), …, sign f_k(x)) ∈ Σ}. A bounded semialgebraic multiset of maximal multiplicity m and complexity (k, ℓ) is a function μ : ℝⁿ → {0, …, m} with bounded support such that each superlevel set {μ ≥ i}, 1 ≤ i ≤ m, has complexity at most (k, ℓ); its lattice count is Σ_{x∈ℤⁿ} μ(x) and its volume is ∫ μ. Every set given by a Boolean combination of at most k polynomial equalities and inequalities of degree ≤ ℓ has complexity at most (k, ℓ).
hypotheses: The sign vector set Σ is arbitrary, so complements, intersections and unions are covered without changing the polynomials.
A multiset counts lattice points with multiplicity; a set is the case m = 1.
proofSteps: Closure properties: complement replaces Σ by its complement; intersection and union of complexity (k, ℓ) and (k', ℓ') sets have complexity (k + k', max(ℓ, ℓ')).

Invertible affine changes of variables x ↦ Ax + b preserve total degree, so u(S), S − v and S/m have the same complexity; restriction to an affine subspace parametrised affinely by ℝ^d gives a set of complexity (k, ℓ) in ℝ^d.

Each complexity-(k, ℓ) set is semialgebraic (a finite Boolean combination of zero and positivity sets of polynomials); conversely a semialgebraic set has some complexity (finitely many polynomials occur in any description).
acceptance: The closed unit ball has complexity (1, 2).
A finite union of h points of ℝ has complexity (1, h).

sources.match: Bounded semialgebraic multisets with maximal multiplicity m defined by at most k polynomial inequalities of degree at most ℓ; the constant of the Davenport estimate depends only on (n, m, k, ℓ).

nodes.title: Uniform bound on connected components in semialgebraic families
nodes.statement: Let S ⊆ ℝ^{m+n} be semialgebraic and for a ∈ ℝ^m let S_a = {x ∈ ℝⁿ : (a, x) ∈ S}. There is M_S ∈ ℕ such that every fibre S_a is a disjoint union of at most M_S cells (in the cylindrical sense), and in particular has at most M_S connected components. Consequently, for all n, k, ℓ there is B(n, k, ℓ) such that every set of complexity at most (k, ℓ) in ℝⁿ has at most B(n, k, ℓ) connected components.
hypotheses: S semialgebraic; the bound M_S depends on S only, not on a.
The consequence uses, for each of the finitely many sign-vector sets Σ ⊆ {−1,0,1}^k, the family parametrised by the coefficient vectors of k polynomials of degree ≤ ℓ.
proofSteps: Take a cylindrical decomposition of ℝ^{m+n} adapted to S (cylindrical algebraic decomposition). Its restriction to each fibre over a ∈ ℝ^m is a decomposition of ℝⁿ into at most as many cells, partitioning S_a.
Cells are connected, so S_a has at most M_S = (number of cells of the decomposition) connected components.

For the consequence: the set {(c, x) : x lies in the complexity-(k, ℓ) set with coefficient vector c and sign set Σ} is semialgebraic in ℝ^{N+n}, N the number of coefficients; take B = the maximum of the M_S over the finitely many Σ.
acceptance: For k = 1, ℓ = 2 in ℝ¹ (sets {sign(ax² + bx + c) ∈ Σ}) every such set has at most 3 components.
The fibres of S = {(a, x) : x² < a} are empty or one interval: M_S = 1 suffices for the component count.

nodes.title: Davenport's interval condition for semialgebraic regions
nodes.statement: Let n, k, ℓ ∈ ℕ and Z ⊆ ℝⁿ of complexity at most (k, ℓ). There is h = h(n, k, ℓ) such that: (a) for every J ⊆ Fin n with |J| ≥ 1 and every line L ⊂ ℝ^J parallel to a coordinate axis, L ∩ π_J(Z) is a union of at most h intervals; (b) for every coordinate i, every J ⊆ Fin n ∖ {i} and every s ≥ 0, the superlevel set {w ∈ ℝ^J : vol_1({t : (t, w) ∈ π_{{i}∪J}(Z)}) ≥ s} of the fibre-length function of π_{{i}∪J}(Z) along the i-th axis satisfies the same condition with the same h. The constant depends on (n, k, ℓ) only.
hypotheses: Z need not be closed; the intervals may be open, half-open or degenerate.
Part (b) is the condition used for triangular unipotent images (unipotent-davenport-transfer).
proofSteps: (a) L ∩ π_J(Z) = π_J(Z ∩ π_J⁻¹(L)), and π_J⁻¹(L) is an affine subspace parametrised affinely by ℝ^{n−|J|+1}; the pulled-back set has complexity (k, ℓ) (semialgebraic-complexity, preimage_affine), hence at most B(n, k, ℓ) connected components (semialgebraic-uniform-components).
A connected set maps under the continuous projection to L onto a connected subset of a line, i.e. an interval; so L ∩ π_J(Z) is a union of at most B intervals.

(b) The set {(c, s, w)} of coefficient vectors, levels s and points w with fibre length ≥ s is semialgebraic (the fibre is a union of boundedly many intervals with semialgebraic endpoints, by Tarski–Seidenberg); apply semialgebraic-uniform-components to this family and argue as in (a).
acceptance: For the open unit disc in ℝ² every axis-parallel line section is one interval and each projection is (−1, 1): h = 1 works.
For a set of complexity (1, ℓ) in ℝ¹, h = ℓ + 1 works.

nodes.title: Davenport's estimate for triangular unipotent images
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, h ≥ 1 and Z ⊆ ℝⁿ bounded such that Z and all its coordinate projections satisfy the h-interval condition on axis-parallel lines, as do the superlevel sets of their fibre-length functions (semialgebraic-interval-condition (b)). Let u be an upper triangular unipotent real matrix. Then |#(uZ ∩ ℤⁿ) − vol(Z)| ≤ C(n, h)·Σ_{J ⊊ Fin n} V_J(Z), with V_∅ = 1 and C(n, h) depending only on n and h. The projection volumes are those of Z, not of uZ. The lower triangular case follows by reversing the order of the coordinates.
hypotheses: Upper triangular means x'_i = x_i + Σ_{j>i} u_ij x_j; the coordinate sheared by the others is the first.
No integrality of u is assumed; vol(uZ) = vol(Z) since det u = 1.
proofSteps: Fibre along the first coordinate: for z ∈ ℝ^{n−1} the fibre of uZ over z is a translate of the fibre of Z over u'⁻¹z, where u' is the lower-right (n − 1)-block of u, again upper triangular unipotent. Hence #(uZ ∩ ℤⁿ) = Σ_{z∈ℤ^{n−1}} (G(u'⁻¹z) + O(h)) with G(w) the length of the fibre of Z over w.
The O(h) terms are supported on u'(π(Z)) ∩ ℤ^{n−1}, π forgetting the first coordinate; by induction (with u') their number is vol(π(Z)) + O(Σ_{J ⊊ {2..n}} V_J(Z)).

Main term: Σ_z G(u'⁻¹z) = ∫_0^∞ #(u'S_s ∩ ℤ^{n−1}) ds with S_s = {G ≥ s}. Apply the induction hypothesis to each S_s: the main terms integrate to ∫ G = vol(Z), and the errors ∫_0^∞ V_J(S_s) ds are at most V_{{1}∪J}(Z), because over each w ∈ π_J(S_s) the projection π_{{1}∪J}(Z) contains a first-coordinate set of length ≥ s.
The superlevel sets S_s are bounded by π(Z) and inherit the interval condition by hypothesis, uniformly in s.
acceptance: u = identity recovers davenport-principle up to the constant.

n = 2, Z = [0, ε] × [0, T], u(x, y) = (x + ay, y): the count is at most 2(⌊T⌋ + 1) for every a, within C·(1 + ε + T) as the lemma predicts, although the projection of uZ to the first axis has length ε + aT.

nodes.title: Lattice points in a ball, by successive minima
nodes.statement: Let Λ is a discrete subgroup of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space E, of rank R ≥ 1, viewed as a full lattice in V = span_ℝ Λ with its induced inner product; λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_R are its successive minima for the closed unit ball of V (GN.1 successive-minimum, one-based here) and det Λ its covolume in V. Then for every T > 0, #(Λ ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ 2^{3R−1}·Σ_{j=0}^{R} T^j/(λ_1⋯λ_j), the j = 0 term being 1. In particular #(Λ ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ 2^{3R−1}(R + 1)·max_{0≤j≤R} T^j/(λ_1⋯λ_j).
hypotheses: No lower bound on T is needed; for T < λ_1 the count is 1 and only the j = 0 term matters.
The constant is explicit; the ambient dimension of E plays no role.
proofSteps: Transport Λ isometrically to a full lattice in ℝ^R (GN.1 successive-minimum-linear-equiv); the minima are unchanged.

Apply Henk's bound to the body K = B̄(0, T), whose minima are λ_i/T (GN.1 successive-minimum-smul-body): #(Λ ∩ K) < 2^{R−1}∏_i(⌊2T/λ_i⌋ + 1) for R ≥ 2 (henk-successive-minima-count), and ≤ ⌊2T/λ_1⌋ + 1 for R = 1 (first-minimum-count).
Each factor is at most 2·max(1, 2T/λ_i). Since the λ_i increase, ∏_i max(1, 2T/λ_i) = max_j ∏_{i≤j} 2T/λ_i ≤ 2^R Σ_j T^j/(λ_1⋯λ_j); collect the powers of 2.
acceptance: Λ = ℤ^R, T = 1: the count is 2R + 1 and the bound is 2^{3R−1}(R + 1).
Λ = aℤ with a > 2T: the count is 1, the j = 0 term.

sources.locator: Lemma 3.5, first bound, p.9 (arXiv:2006.02356v1), citing Schmidt, Duke Math. J. 35 (1968), Lemma 2
sources.match: The count of lattice points of a rank-R lattice in a ball of radius T ≥ 1 is ≪_R Σ_i T^{R−i}/(λ_1⋯λ_{R−i}).

The same estimate for a bounded domain, quoted from Schmidt; see bounded-domain-count.

nodes.title: Ball count past an intermediate minimum
nodes.statement: Let Λ is a discrete subgroup of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space E, of rank R ≥ 1, viewed as a full lattice in V = span_ℝ Λ with its induced inner product; λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_R are its successive minima for the closed unit ball of V (GN.1 successive-minimum, one-based here) and det Λ its covolume in V. If 1 ≤ i₀ ≤ R and T ≥ λ_{i₀}, then #(Λ ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ C_R·T^R/(λ_1⋯λ_{i₀−1}·λ_{i₀}^{R−i₀+1}), with C_R = 2^{3R−1}(R + 1).
hypotheses: T ≥ λ_{i₀} is required: for smaller T the right-hand side can be smaller than 1.
proofSteps: Start from ball-count-successive-minima. For j ≤ i₀ − 1 bound T^j/(λ_1⋯λ_j) by T^R/(λ_1⋯λ_{i₀−1}λ_{i₀}^{R−i₀+1}) using T ≥ λ_{i₀} ≥ λ_i (i ≤ i₀); for j ≥ i₀ use λ_i ≥ λ_{i₀} for i ≥ i₀.
Sum the R + 1 terms.
acceptance: i₀ = R: the bound reads T^R/(λ_1⋯λ_R) ≍ T^R/det Λ, the volume order.
i₀ = 1: T^R/λ_1^R.

sources.locator: Lemma 3.5, second bound and its proof, pp.9–10
sources.match: For i₀ ∈ {1, …, R} and T ≥ λ_{i₀}, the count is ≪_R T^R/(λ_1⋯λ_{i₀−1}λ_{i₀}^{R−i₀+1}).

nodes.title: Schmidt's count in a dilated bounded domain
nodes.statement: Let Λ be a lattice of rank k in ℝ^m with Euclidean successive minima μ_1 ≤ … ≤ μ_k, and D ⊆ ℝ^m bounded. There is C = C(k, D) with #(Y·D ∩ Λ) ≤ C·max_{0≤j≤k} Y^j/(μ_1⋯μ_j) for every Y > 0; the j = 0 term is 1. Without the j = 0 term the bound is false whenever 0 ∈ D: the origin is always counted while every other term tends to 0 as Y → 0.
hypotheses: The j = 0 term is necessary: for 0 ∈ D the origin is always counted.
proofSteps: Choose r with D ⊆ B̄(0, r); then #(YD ∩ Λ) ≤ #(Λ ∩ B̄(0, rY)).
Apply ball-count-successive-minima and bound (rY)^j by max(1, r)^k Y^j.
acceptance: Λ = ℤ^k, D = (−1, 1)^k, Y → 0: the count is 1 = the j = 0 term while every other term tends to 0.

sources.locator: Proposition 5.2, (22), p.22 (published Forum Math. Pi version; (21) in arXiv v1)
sources.match: States the bound with the maximum over 1 ≤ j ≤ k; the corrected range 0 ≤ j ≤ k is PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-25/E14 (confirmed).
The ball case.

nodes.title: Counting vectors of bounded norm in a definite quadratic lattice
nodes.statement: Let (L, Q) be a free ℤ-module of rank r ≥ 1 with a positive definite quadratic form Q (real-valued). Let μ_i = inf{y > 0 : L contains i linearly independent vectors v with Q(v) ≤ y²} and a_i = μ_1⋯μ_i (a_0 = 1), as in GN.1 successive-minimum-partial-product. Then for every Y > 0, #{v ∈ L : Q(v) ≤ Y} ≤ 2^{3r−1}Σ_{i=0}^{r} Y^{i/2}/a_i; the nonzero count vanishes for Y < μ_1².
hypotheses: Q positive definite on L ⊗ ℝ; the minima are in the square-root normalisation of Eskin–Katznelson.
proofSteps: Give L ⊗ ℝ the inner product with ‖v‖² = Q(v); then L is a full lattice whose Euclidean minima are the μ_i.
Apply ball-count-successive-minima with T = √Y.
acceptance: L = ℤ^r with Q = sum of squares: μ_i = 1, a_i = 1 and the bound is a polynomial in √Y of degree r, matching the order Y^{r/2} of the true count.

sources.locator: Proof of Propositions 7.11 and 7.13 (accepted version of 25 December 2021), quoting Eskin–Katznelson, Lemma 2.4 and (5)–(6)
sources.match: Counts vectors of bounded Q in the lattices L_n by Σ_i Y^{i/2}/a_i with a constant depending on the rank only.

sources.locator: Proof of Proposition 7.7 and footnote 32, p.40 (arXiv:1909.07473v3)
sources.match: The count of nonzero v with Q(v) < X is ≪_r Σ_i X^{i/2}/a_i.

nodes.title: Counting nonzero vectors below the last minimum
nodes.statement: Let Λ is a discrete subgroup of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space E, of rank R ≥ 1, viewed as a full lattice in V = span_ℝ Λ with its induced inner product; λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_R are its successive minima for the closed unit ball of V (GN.1 successive-minimum, one-based here) and det Λ its covolume in V. Let M > 0 with M < λ_1 and Y ≥ λ_R. (a) For 0 ≤ R₀ ≤ R − 1 and 0 < T ≤ Y: #((Λ ∖ {0}) ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ C_R·(T^{R−R₀}Y^{R₀}/det Λ + (T/M)^{R−R₀−1}). (b) If moreover 0 ≤ j₀ ≤ R − 1, J ≥ M with J < λ_{j₀+1}, and 0 ≤ R₀ ≤ R − 1 − j₀, then #((Λ ∖ {0}) ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ C_R·(T^{R−R₀}Y^{R₀}/det Λ + (T/M)^{j₀}·((T/J)^{R−R₀−1−j₀} + 1)).
hypotheses: C_R depends only on R.
If T ≤ M the left side is 0, so only T > M matters.
proofSteps: (a) is (b) with j₀ = 0, J = M.

For T > M write the count via ball-count-successive-minima and split the sum at R₀: the terms with many minima use λ_{R−i+1}⋯λ_R ≤ Y^i and Minkowski's second theorem λ_1⋯λ_R ≍ det Λ; the others use λ_i > M for i ≤ j₀ and λ_i > J for i > j₀.
Sum the geometric series in T/J (T > M) as in the source.
acceptance: Λ = ℤ^R, M = 1/2, Y = 1, T = 1/4: the count is 0.
R = 1: (a) with R₀ = 0 gives a bound C(T/det Λ + 1).

sources.match: States both bounds with implied constants depending at most on R and proves them from Lemma 3.5 and Minkowski's second theorem.

nodes.title: A basis adapted to the successive minima, with coordinate bounds
nodes.statement: Let Λ be a full lattice in an R-dimensional real inner-product space E (R ≥ 1) with successive minima λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_R. There is a ℤ-basis b_1, …, b_R of Λ with ‖b_j‖ ≤ j·λ_j for every j, and every x = Σ_j t_j b_j ∈ E satisfies |t_j| ≤ c_R‖x‖/λ_j for every j, where c_R = 2^R·R!/V_R and V_R is the volume of the unit ball.
hypotheses: The coordinate bound holds for all real x, not only lattice points.
The basis need not realise the minima.
proofSteps: The basis comes from GN.1 basis-from-minima: b_j lies in (λ_1 + ⋯ + λ_j)·B̄, so ‖b_j‖ ≤ jλ_j.
Cramer's rule: t_j = det(b_1, …, x, …, b_R)/det(b_1, …, b_R), x in place j; Hadamard's inequality bounds the numerator by ‖x‖∏_{i≠j}‖b_i‖ ≤ ‖x‖∏_{i≠j} iλ_i.
det(b) = det Λ ≥ V_R λ_1⋯λ_R/2^R by Minkowski's second theorem; combine.
acceptance: E = ℝ^R, Λ = ℤ^R: the standard basis satisfies both bounds with t_j = x_j.
R = 1, Λ = aℤ: b_1 = a and t_1 = x/a.

sources.locator: Proofs of Lemmas 3.21 (pp.22–23) and 3.23 (p.24), citing Davenport, Proc. Roy. Soc. A 272 (1963), Lemma 5
sources.match: Uses a basis with ‖b_j‖ ≍ λ_j in which every vector x of the lattice has coordinates of size ≪ ‖x‖/λ_j.

The basis-from-minima input.

nodes.title: Widmer's lattice-point count for Lipschitz boundaries
nodes.statement: Let D ≥ 1, Λ a full lattice in ℝ^D with Euclidean successive minima λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_D, and S ⊆ ℝ^D bounded whose boundary ∂S is covered by the images of M maps [0,1]^{D−1} → ℝ^D, each Lipschitz with constant L (∂S is Lipschitz parametrisable in dimension D − 1 with these data). Then S is Lebesgue measurable and |#(S ∩ Λ) − vol(S)/det Λ| ≤ c₀(D)·M·max_{0≤i<D} L^i/(λ_1⋯λ_i), where the i = 0 term is 1 and c₀(D) = D^{3D²/2}.
hypotheses: The bound is uniform in Λ: it depends on Λ only through its minima, unlike the fixed-lattice count of GlobalNumberFields Layer 3.
For D = 1 the boundary is a finite set of at most M points.
proofSteps: Measurability: ∂S is a finite union of Lipschitz images of a (D−1)-cube, hence Lebesgue null.

Choose a basis with minimal orthogonality defect (adapted-basis-coordinates) and its fundamental parallelepiped P; #(S ∩ Λ) differs from vol(S)/det Λ by at most the number of translates of P meeting ∂S.

Cover each Lipschitz image by subcubes of side 1/m; each subimage has diameter ≤ L√(D−1)/m and meets a number of translates bounded by ∏_i(κL/(mλ_i) + 2) with κ the orthogonality constant; optimise m to get the maximum over i.
acceptance: Λ = ℤ^D, S = [0, N]^D: the error is (N + 1)^D − N^D ≤ c₀(D)·2D·N^{D−1}, consistent with M = 2D faces of Lipschitz constant ≍ N.
Λ = εℤ ⊕ ℤ^{D−1} with ε → 0 and S fixed: the bound grows like L/ε, the i = 1 term.

sources.locator: Theorem 5.4 and its proof, p.17 (arXiv:1204.0927; Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 362 (2010))
sources.match: For a lattice in ℝ^D with minima λ_i and bounded S whose boundary lies in Lip(D, 1, M, L), S is measurable and the count differs from vol S/det Λ by at most c₀(D)M max_{0≤i<D} L^i/(λ_1⋯λ_i), with c₀(D) = D^{3D²/2}.
Applies Widmer's Theorem 5.4 to dilated cubes in a family of lattices Λ_g, uniformly in g.

nodes.title: Lattice points in semialgebraic families, uniformly in the lattice
nodes.statement: Let m, n ≥ 1 and Z ⊆ ℝ^{m+n} semialgebraic with bounded fibres Z_T = {x : (T, x) ∈ Z}, T ∈ ℝ^m. There is c_Z depending only on Z such that for every full lattice Λ ⊆ ℝⁿ with successive minima λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_n and every T: |#(Z_T ∩ Λ) − vol(Z_T)/det Λ| ≤ c_Z·Σ_{j=0}^{n−1} V_j(Z_T)/(λ_1⋯λ_j), with V_j the coordinate projection volumes (V_0 = 1).
hypotheses: Only semialgebraic families are claimed here; the source proves the statement for families definable in any o-minimal structure, which no library or roadmap plans.
proofSteps: Map Λ to ℤⁿ by the linear map Ψ sending an adapted basis (adapted-basis-coordinates) to the standard basis; apply davenport-principle to Ψ(closure Z_T) with a Davenport constant h depending only on Z (semialgebraic-interval-condition applied to the family, via semialgebraic-uniform-components).
Bound V_j(Ψ(Z_T)) by a constant times V_j(Z_T)/(λ_1⋯λ_j) using the column bounds of Ψ⁻¹ (Thunder's argument, Barroero–Widmer Lemmas 2.2–2.4).
Pass from closures to Z_T: the boundary of a semialgebraic fibre has lower dimension and its lattice points are counted by the same bound.
acceptance: Λ = ℤⁿ and Z_T = T·[0,1]ⁿ (T ∈ ℝ_{>0}): recovers |(⌊T⌋ + 1)ⁿ − Tⁿ| ≪ Σ_j T^j.
The example of Barroero–Widmer p.5 (union of axis segments of length T shifted by λ_j e_j) shows the j-th term cannot be dropped.

sources.match: For a definable family with bounded fibres, |#(Z_T ∩ Λ) − vol(Z_T)/det Λ| ≤ c_Z Σ_{j<n} V_j(Z_T)/(λ_1⋯λ_j); semialgebraic families are definable.
Uses Theorem 1.3 of Barroero–Widmer for the semialgebraic regions R_v(T, γ).

nodes.title: Angular bands and their lattice regions
nodes.statement: Let N ≥ 1, γ > 0 and v ∈ ℝ^N. The angular band of v is C_v^{(γ)} = {t ∈ ℝ^N : |⟨v, t⟩| ≤ ‖v‖·‖t‖/(2γ)}, the set of vectors making an angle with the hyperplane v^⊥ whose sine is at most 1/(2γ). For v_1, …, v_I ∈ ℝ^N and T > 0 put R_v(T, γ) = B̄_N(T) ∩ C_{v_1}^{(γ)} ∩ ⋯ ∩ C_{v_I}^{(γ)}, and for a lattice Λ of rank R put V_v(Λ; γ) = vol_R(span_ℝ Λ ∩ R_v(1, γ)), the R-dimensional volume in the span.
hypotheses: γ > 0; v = 0 gives the whole space (the inequality reads 0 ≤ 0).
The band is a closed cone (invariant under t ↦ ct for c ∈ ℝ), so R_v(T, γ) = T·R_v(1, γ).
proofSteps: The band is defined by the polynomial inequality 4γ²⟨v,t⟩² ≤ ‖v‖²‖t‖², so R_v(T, γ) has complexity (I + 1, 2) (semialgebraic-complexity).
Homogeneity: C_v^{(γ)} is closed under real scalar multiplication, hence R_v(T, γ) = T·R_v(1, γ) and V_v depends on Λ only through span_ℝ Λ.
acceptance: For N = 2, v = e_1 and γ = 1/2 the band is all of ℝ² (|t_1| ≤ ‖t‖ always).
For N = 2, v = e_1, γ = 1 the band is {|t_1| ≤ ‖t‖/2}, two sectors of half-angle π/6 around the t_2-axis.

nodes.title: Lattice points in intersections of angular bands
nodes.statement: Let N ≥ 2, 1 ≤ R ≤ N, 1 ≤ I ≤ N − 1, Λ ⊆ ℝ^N a lattice of rank R, v_1, …, v_I ∈ ℝ^N and γ > 0. Let Y ≥ λ_R(Λ). For T ≥ Y: #(Λ ∩ R_v(T, γ)) = (T^R/det Λ)·(V_v(Λ; γ) + O(Y/T)), the implied constant depending only on N and I (and on R).
hypotheses: The constant is uniform in Λ, the v_i and γ.
The source states dependence on R only; the uniformity in the family follows from the semialgebraic family bound, whose constant depends on the family (N, I): recorded as a dependence on (N, I).
proofSteps: Rotate span_ℝ Λ onto ℝ^R × {0} by an orthogonal map; the region becomes a semialgebraic family in the parameters (v, γ, T) of complexity depending only on (N, I).
Apply semialgebraic-family-lattice-count: the error is ≪ Σ_{i=1}^{R} T^{R−i}/(λ_1⋯λ_{R−i}).
By Minkowski's second theorem λ_1⋯λ_{R−i} ≍ det Λ/(λ_{R−i+1}⋯λ_R) ≥ det Λ/Y^i, so each error term is ≪ (T^R/det Λ)(Y/T)^i ≤ (T^R/det Λ)(Y/T) for T ≥ Y.
acceptance: I = 1, v_1 = 0: the region is the ball, V_v = V_R and the formula is the classical ball count with error T^{R−1}Y/det Λ.

nodes.title: Primitive integral lattices with prescribed dyadic minima
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, 1 ≤ r ≤ n + 1 and s_1, …, s_r ≥ 1. S_{r,n}(s_1, …, s_r) is the set of primitive lattices L ⊆ ℤ^{n+1} of rank r (L = span_ℝ L ∩ ℤ^{n+1}) whose Euclidean successive minima satisfy s_j/2 < λ_j(L) ≤ s_j for every j.
hypotheses: Primitive means saturated in ℤ^{n+1}; the minima are computed in span_ℝ L.
proofSteps: A rank-r primitive lattice is determined by its real span, so S_{r,n} is a set of rational subspaces of dimension r.
Finiteness: λ_r(L) ≤ s_r bounds a basis of L, so only finitely many L occur (ball-count-successive-minima).
acceptance: S_{1,n}(s) is the set of lines ℤx with x primitive and s/2 < ‖x‖ ≤ s.
For r = n + 1 the only primitive lattice is ℤ^{n+1}, with all minima 1: it lies in S_{n+1,n}(s) iff 1 ≤ s_j < 2 for all j.

nodes.title: Primitive extensions of a fixed primitive lattice
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, 2 ≤ r ≤ n + 1 and L' ⊆ ℤ^{n+1} a primitive lattice of rank r − 1. For s ≥ 1, the number of primitive lattices L ⊆ ℤ^{n+1} of rank r with L' ⊆ L and det(L)/det(L') ≤ s is ≪_n s^{n−r+2}·det(L').
hypotheses: The implied constant depends only on n.
proofSteps: L ↦ π(L) with π the orthogonal projection away from span L' identifies such L with primitive vectors of the rank-(n − r + 2) quotient lattice π(ℤ^{n+1}) of norm ≤ s, up to sign (det L = det L'·‖π(x)‖).

M = π(ℤ^{n+1}) has rank q = n − r + 2, determinant 1/det(L') (GN.0 covolume-projection) and integral dual M* = L'^⊥ (GN.0 dual-projection-comap). Integrality gives λ_i(M*) ≥ 1, so transference-minkowski-constant bounds every minimum μ_i of M by a constant c(q).
By ball-count-successive-minima the number of x ∈ M with ‖x‖ ≤ s is ≪ Σ_j s^j/(μ_1⋯μ_j) = Σ_j s^j μ_{j+1}⋯μ_q/(μ_1⋯μ_q) ≪ s^q·det(L') for s ≥ 1, using μ_1⋯μ_q ≍ det M (Minkowski's second theorem).
acceptance: r = 2, L' = ℤe_1: the extensions correspond to primitive x ∈ ℤ^n (the other coordinates) with ‖x‖ ≤ s, about s^n of them.

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.18, p.19, citing Schmidt, Duke Math. J. 35 (1968), Lemma 6 with i = 1

nodes.statement: For N ≥ 2 and w, z ∈ ℝ^N let I(w, z) = vol_{N−1}{t ∈ (ℝw)^⊥ : |⟨z, t⟩| ≤ ‖t‖ ≤ 1} (volume in the hyperplane w^⊥, w ≠ 0) and J(w, z) = vol_N{t ∈ ℝ^N : |⟨w, t⟩| ≤ ‖t‖, |⟨z, t⟩| ≤ ‖t‖, ‖t‖ ≤ 1}. Put δ(w, z) = ‖w‖²‖z‖² − ⟨w, z⟩², which is > 0 exactly when w, z are linearly independent.

δ(w, z) = 0 for dependent vectors.

nodes.title: Asymptotics of the band section volumes
nodes.statement: Let N ≥ 3 and w, z ∈ ℝ^N linearly independent, δ = δ(w, z). Then I(w, z) = (2(N − 2)/(N − 1))·V_{N−2}·‖w‖/δ^{1/2}·(1 + O_N(min{1, ‖w‖²/δ})), and J(w, z) = (4(N − 2)/N)·V_{N−2}/δ^{1/2}·(1 + O_N(min{1, (‖w‖ + ‖z‖)²/δ})).
hypotheses: N ≥ 3; the asymptotics are informative when δ is large compared with ‖w‖² (resp. (‖w‖+‖z‖)²).
proofSteps: I: inside w^⊥ the condition |⟨z, t⟩| ≤ ‖t‖ is a band around the hyperplane orthogonal to the component z' of z in w^⊥, with ‖z'‖ = δ^{1/2}/‖w‖; integrate in polar coordinates, the band having angular measure ≍ 1/‖z'‖ with the explicit constant 2V_{N−2}(N−2)/(N−1).

J: intersect two such bands; for δ large the intersection is a neighbourhood of the codimension-2 subspace {w, z}^⊥ of angular size ≍ 1/(δ^{1/2}) after the change of variables to an orthonormal basis of span(w, z).
acceptance: When w ⊥ z with ‖w‖ = 1 and ‖z‖ = R large, I ≈ 2(N − 2)V_{N−2}/((N − 1)R).

S*_0(Λ; B̄(T)) counts primitive points; S_0 counts all nonzero points.

nodes.title: Primitive points of a primitive lattice in a ball
nodes.statement: Let N ≥ 3, 3 ≤ R ≤ N, Λ ⊆ ℤ^N a primitive lattice of rank R and Y ≥ 1 such that B̄_N(Y) contains R linearly independent vectors of Λ (λ_R(Λ) ≤ Y). For T ≥ Y: S*_0(Λ; B̄_N(T)) = V_R T^R/(ζ(R) det Λ)·(1 + O_R(Y/T)) + O_R(T log(2Y)).
hypotheses: Primitive Λ, so primitivity in Λ and in ℤ^N agree; R ≥ 3 makes the Möbius sum converge with a log error.
proofSteps: Möbius inversion over the content: S*_0(Λ; B̄(T)) = Σ_{m ≥ 1} μ(m)·#((Λ ∖ {0}) ∩ B̄(T/m)).
For m ≤ T/Y use the ball count with error (band-count with I = 1, v = 0): #(Λ ∩ B̄(T/m)) = V_R(T/m)^R/det Λ·(1 + O(mY/T)); for m > T/Y bound by small-vector-count.

nodes.title: Symmetric matrices with prescribed row space
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2 and S = Sym²(n) the real symmetric n×n matrices with the Frobenius Euclidean norm (identify S with ℝ^{n(n+1)/2} so that off-diagonal coordinates carry weight √2; covolumes are taken for this norm). For a lattice Λ ⊆ ℤⁿ of rank r, S(Λ) is the set of B ∈ S(ℤ) whose row space is contained in Λ ⊗ ℝ, and S'(Λ) the lattice it spans; the full-rank part S(Λ)^{full} consists of those B whose row space is all of Λ ⊗ ℝ. For v, w ∈ ℝⁿ put v ∗ w = vwᵀ + wvᵀ if v, w are linearly independent and v ∗ w = vwᵀ otherwise. For s = diag(t_1^{−1}, …, t_n^{−1}) with t_i > 0 and 1 ≤ r < n put C(r, s) = ∏_{1≤i<j≤n, j>n−r} t_i/t_j. SL_n(ℝ) acts on S by γ·A = γAγᵀ.
hypotheses: The full-rank subset and the spanning lattice are different objects (PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-25/E18); counts of rank-r matrices fibre over the saturated row lattice.
C(r, s) is a product over the pairs (i, j) with i < j and j > n − r.
proofSteps: v ∗ w is symmetric with row space in span{v, w} and ‖v‖‖w‖ ≤ ‖v ∗ w‖ ≤ 2‖v‖‖w‖ in the Frobenius norm.
Every rank-r integral symmetric matrix has a unique saturated row lattice Λ = rowspace ∩ ℤⁿ, primitive of rank r, and lies in S(Λ)^{full}.
γ(S(Λ)) = {γBγᵀ : B ∈ S(Λ)} has row spaces in γΛ ⊗ ℝ.
acceptance: For n = 2, Λ = ℤe_1: S(Λ) = {diag(b, 0) : b ∈ ℤ} = ℤ·e_1 ∗ e_1/1 (here e_1 ∗ e_1 = e_1e_1ᵀ).

nodes.title: A reduced basis for the symmetric row lattice
nodes.statement: Let γ ∈ SL_n(ℝ), Λ ⊆ ℤⁿ primitive of rank r and ℓ_1, …, ℓ_r a basis of γΛ. Then {ℓ_i ∗ ℓ_j : 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ r} is a basis of γ(S'(Λ)), and the covolume of γ(S'(Λ)) in its span is 2^{r(r−1)/4}·d(γΛ)^{r+1}, where d(γΛ) is the covolume of γΛ in its span. If {ℓ_i} is almost reduced (∏‖ℓ_i‖ ≪_n d(γΛ)), so is {ℓ_i ∗ ℓ_j}.
hypotheses: d(γΛ) ≠ d(Λ) in general: an element of SL_n(ℝ) preserves n-dimensional covolume only (PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-25/E15).
Almost reduced bases exist (adapted-basis-coordinates).
proofSteps: Choose a ℤ-basis e_1, …, e_r of Λ; S'(Λ) is the image of Sym²(ℤ^r) under X ↦ EXEᵀ, E the n×r matrix of the basis, with basis {e_i ∗ e_j}.
Apply γ: γ(e_i ∗ e_j)γᵀ = γe_i ∗ γe_j, and change basis within γΛ.

Covolume: the map Sym²(ℝ^r) → S, X ↦ FXFᵀ (F the matrix of ℓ) scales Frobenius covolume by det(FᵀF)^{(r+1)/2} = d(γΛ)^{r+1}; the factor 2^{r(r−1)/4} comes from the √2 weights of the off-diagonal coordinates against the basis vectors ℓ_i ∗ ℓ_j.
acceptance: r = 1, Λ = ℤv: S'(Λ) = ℤ·vvᵀ, covolume ‖vvᵀ‖ = ‖v‖² = d(Λ)², matching 2^0 d^2.

sources.locator: Theorem 5.3, p.22 (published), following Eskin–Katznelson, Duke Math. J. 79 (1995), Proposition 3.3 and Lemma 3.5
sources.match: States the basis, the covolume formula and the transfer of almost-reducedness; the published text writes the covolume also as 2^{r(r−1)/4}d(Λ)^{r+1}, valid only for γ preserving r-dimensional covolume (E15).

nodes.title: Minima conditions for a nonempty count
nodes.statement: Let γ ∈ SL_n(ℝ), Λ ⊆ ℤⁿ primitive of rank r with γΛ having successive minima μ_1 ≤ … ≤ μ_r, D ⊆ S(ℝ) bounded and Y > 0. If Y·D ∩ γ(S(Λ)^{full}) ≠ ∅ then μ_iμ_j ≤ c_1Y for all i, j with i + j ≤ r + 1, with c_1 depending on n and D.
hypotheses: The nonempty intersection is with the full-rank part: a matrix whose row space is all of γΛ ⊗ ℝ (E18).
proofSteps: Write a full-rank B ∈ YD ∩ γ(S(Λ)) as Σ_{k≤l} b_kl ℓ_k ∗ ℓ_l in an almost reduced basis ℓ of γΛ. If μ_iμ_j > c_1Y for some i + j ≤ r + 1, every basis vector ℓ_k ∗ ℓ_l with k ≥ i, l ≥ j has length ≥ μ_kμ_l > c_1Y, so its coefficient vanishes (almost-reducedness bounds |b_kl| by ‖B‖/‖ℓ_k ∗ ℓ_l‖ up to a constant).
Then the Gram matrix of B in the basis ℓ has a zero block in rows i..r and columns j..r, of total size (r − i + 1) + (r − j + 1) ≥ r + 1 > r, so B has rank < r, a contradiction.
The pigeonhole on the anti-diagonal i + j = r + 1 is Eskin–Katznelson's Lemma 4.1.
acceptance: r = 1: the condition is μ_1² ≤ c_1Y, i.e. the generator of γΛ has ‖v‖² ≪ Y.

sources.match: If the count is positive then µ_iµ_j ≤ c_1Y for i + j ≤ r + 1.

nodes.title: Counting symmetric matrices with a fixed row lattice
nodes.statement: Let γ ∈ SL_n(ℝ), Λ ⊆ ℤⁿ primitive of rank r with γΛ having minima μ_1 ≤ … ≤ μ_r, D ⊆ S(ℝ) bounded and Y ≥ 1. Then #(Y·D ∩ γ(S(Λ)^{full})) ≪_{n,D} (Y^{r(r+1)/2}/d(γΛ)^{r+1})·∏_{1≤i<j≤r, i+j≤r+1} μ_j/μ_i.
hypotheses: The denominator is d(γΛ)^{r+1}, not d(Λ)^{r+1} (E15).
Counting is over the full-rank part; the spanning lattice S'(Λ) is used only for the lattice-point bound.
proofSteps: By bounded-domain-count and eskin-katznelson-basis, the count in S'(Λ) is ≪ (Y^{r(r+1)/2}/d(γΛ)^{r+1})·∏_{(i,j)∈U(r)}(Y/(μ_iμ_j))^{−1}, U(r) = {i ≤ j, i + j > r + 1} (the minima of γ(S'(Λ)) above Y).

If the full-rank count is positive, eskin-katznelson-nonvanishing gives μ_{r+1−j}μ_j ≪ Y, and the injection (i, j) ↦ (r + 1 − j, i) of U(r) into {k < l, k + l ≤ r + 1} turns the product into ∏ μ_j/μ_i over the stated pairs.
acceptance: r = 1: the bound is Y/d(γΛ)² = Y/μ_1², the count of b with |b|μ_1² ≪ Y.

sources.match: States the bound with d(Λ)^{r+1} in the denominator; the correct quantity is d(γΛ)^{r+1} (PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-25/E15, confirmed).

nodes.title: Counting row lattices with prescribed skew minima
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, 1 ≤ r < n, s = diag(t_1^{−1}, …, t_n^{−1}) with t_1 ≥ c t_2 ≥ ⋯ (s in the Siegel torus T′: t_i ≫ t_{i+1}) and L = (L_1, …, L_r) with 0 < L_1 ≤ ⋯ ≤ L_r. Let Σ(L, s) be the set of primitive Λ ⊆ ℤⁿ of rank r whose minima μ_i of s^{−1}Λ satisfy L_i ≤ μ_i < 2L_i. (a) If Σ(L, s) ≠ ∅ then L_i t_j^{−1} > c' for all i + j ≥ n + 1, with c' depending only on n. (b) #Σ(L, s) ≪_n (L_1⋯L_r)^n·∏_{1≤i<j≤r}(L_i/L_j)·C(r, s).
hypotheses: The ordering t_1 ≫ ⋯ ≫ t_n is part of the hypothesis (s ∈ T′).
proofSteps: (a) A basis ℓ_1, …, ℓ_r of Λ with |s^{−1}ℓ_i| < 2L_i has integral entries u_ij with |u_ij| ≤ 2L_it_j^{−1}. If L_kt_{n+1−k}^{−1} < c'' for some k and a small c'', then |u_ij| < 1, so u_ij = 0, for all i ≤ k and j ≤ n + 1 − k (L_it_j^{−1} ≪ L_kt_{n+1−k}^{−1} there); thus ℓ_1, …, ℓ_k lie in the (k − 1)-dimensional span of e_{n+2−k}, …, e_n, contradicting independence.

(b) Count r-tuples (ℓ_1, …, ℓ_r) in s^{−1}ℤⁿ with L_i ≤ |ℓ_i| < 2L_i forming a reduced basis: for each i the coordinates j ≤ α(i) (with L_i t_{α(i)}^{−1} ≤ c') vanish, and bounded-domain-count bounds the choices of ℓ_i in the remaining coordinates; (a) gives α(i) ≤ n − i; multiply and compare with C(r, s).
acceptance: s = 1 (all t_i = 1): (b) reads #Σ ≪ (L_1⋯L_r)^n∏(L_i/L_j), the count of primitive rank-r lattices with minima ≍ L_i (compare primitive-lattice-minima-count).

sources.locator: Lemma 5.6, Proposition 5.7 and proofs, (27)–(28), pp.23–24 (published; Lemma 5.6 and (27) in arXiv v1)
sources.match: Lemma 5.6 gives the condition L_it_j^{−1} > c′ for i + j ≥ n + 1; Proposition 5.7 bounds #Σ(L, s).

nodes.title: Singular integral symmetric matrices in skewed balls
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, 1 ≤ r < n, Θ > 0, D ⊆ S(ℝ) bounded, Y > 1 and s = diag(t_1^{−1}, …, t_n^{−1}) ∈ T′ with t_1 ≤ C·Y^Θ and t_n ≥ c·Y^{−Θ}. Let N_r(Y, s) = #(s(Y·D) ∩ S(ℤ)^{(r)}), S(ℤ)^{(r)} the integral symmetric matrices of rank exactly r. Then N_r(Y, s) ≪_{n,Θ,D} C(r, s)·Y^{nr/2}·(log Y)^r, uniformly in s.
hypotheses: The endpoint constraints t_1 ≪ Y^Θ, t_n ≫ Y^{−Θ} make the number of dyadic ranges O((log Y)^r).
proofSteps: Fibre the rank-r matrices by their saturated row lattice Λ (symmetric-row-lattices): N_r(Y, s) = Σ_Λ #(Y·D ∩ s^{−1}(S(Λ)^{full})) after transporting by γ = s^{−1}.
Decompose the Λ dyadically by the minima of s^{−1}Λ (sets Σ(L, s)); eskin-katznelson-nonvanishing and skew-row-lattice-count (a) confine L to O((log Y)^r) dyadic boxes.
For each box combine row-lattice-matrix-count with d(s^{−1}Λ) ≍ L_1⋯L_r and skew-row-lattice-count (b); the product telescopes to C(r, s)Y^{nr/2}.
acceptance: s = 1: N_r(Y, 1) ≪ Y^{nr/2}(log Y)^r, the Eskin–Katznelson upper bound for rank-r symmetric matrices of norm ≤ Y.

sources.locator: Theorem 5.1, p.21, and its proof, pp.24–25 (published)
sources.match: States N_r(Y, s) = O(C(r, s)Y^{nr/2} log^r Y) uniformly for s ∈ T′ with t_1 ≪ Y^Θ, t_n ≫ Y^{−Θ}; proved by summing Proposition 5.5 over dyadic ranges using Proposition 5.7.

nodes.title: Planar domains with a curvature-controlled lattice count
nodes.statement: A C² convex planar domain is a compact convex E ⊆ ℝ² with nonempty interior whose boundary is a C² curve of nowhere vanishing curvature; A(E) is its area and R_max(E) the maximum radius of curvature of ∂E. For C > 0 and θ > 0, L(C, θ) is the class of C² convex planar domains E such that for every integer a ≥ 1 and every x₀ ∈ ℤ² with A(E) ≥ a²: |#(a^{−1}(E − x₀) ∩ ℤ²) − a^{−2}A(E)| ≤ C·(R_max(E)/a)^θ. An exponent θ is admissible (for integral binary forms) if some C makes every ellipse {Q ≤ X}, Q a positive definite integral binary quadratic form and X > 0, belong to L(C, θ).
hypotheses: The estimate is uniform over integer translates x₀ and integer scalings a, as the sieve applications require.
Ellipses of definite integral binary forms have analytic boundary of nonzero curvature.

nodes.title: Van der Corput's bound for C² convex domains
nodes.statement: There is an absolute constant C such that for every C² convex planar domain E (nonvanishing curvature, maximal radius of curvature r_max), every real x ≥ 1 and every translate: |#(x·E ∩ ℤ²) − x²A(E)| ≤ C(1 + r_max·x)^{2/3}. Consequently, for every ε > 0 every C² convex domain lies in L(C_ε, 2/3 + ε) for some C_ε, and every θ > 2/3 is admissible.
hypotheses: The constant is absolute (Chaix's form); translates are covered since the hypotheses are translation-invariant.
proofSteps: Cut ∂(xE) into arcs on which the boundary is a graph y = f(t) with |f''| ≍ 1/(r x) bounded above and below; the count in each vertical strip is Σ_t (⌊f(t)⌋ − …) and the error is Σ ψ(f(t)) with ψ the sawtooth.
Van der Corput's second-derivative test bounds Σ_{t∈I} ψ(f(t)) ≪ |I|λ^{1/3} + λ^{−1/2} with λ ≍ 1/(r_max x) the size of f''; summing over O(1) arcs of length ≪ r_max x gives (r_max x)^{2/3}.
The class statement: with x = 1/a after translating by x₀, (R_max/a)^{2/3} ≥ 1 when A(E) ≥ a², so the additive 1 is absorbed.
acceptance: The circle of radius √X: the error is O(X^{1/3}), the classical Gauss circle exponent of van der Corput.
Jarník's convex curves show the exponent 2/3 cannot be improved for general C² domains.

sources.match: States P(x; CD₂) ≪ x^{2/3} for C² boundaries, Chaix's form |P| ≤ C(1 + r_max x)^{2/3} with absolute C, Krätzel's explicit constants, and Jarník's optimality.
Deduces from van der Corput's bound that every C² convex domain lies in L(C_l, 2/3 + ε).

nodes.title: Huxley's bound for C³ convex domains
nodes.statement: For every C³ convex planar domain E (boundary of class C³ with nonvanishing curvature) there is C_E such that |#(x·E ∩ ℤ²) − x²A(E)| ≤ C_E·x^{131/208}(log x)^{18637/8320} for x ≥ 2. For ellipses the constant can be taken uniform in the form after normalising the radius of curvature, so every θ > 131/208 is admissible.
hypotheses: C³ boundary; the uniformity for ellipses of integral forms is what admissibility requires.
proofSteps: The proof is Huxley's discrete Hardy–Littlewood method (Bombieri–Iwaniec–Huxley) for the sawtooth sums Σψ(f(t)), with first and second spacing problems for resonance curves. The method is not decomposed here; see the gap 'Huxley exponent-sum method'.

sources.match: States Huxley's 1993 bound x^{46/73} for C³ boundaries and his 2003 improvement x^{131/208}(log x)^{18637/8320}.

nodes.title: Points of a Markoff level set with a fixed first coordinate
nodes.statement: For integers a with 3 ≤ a ≪ K^{1/3}, let N_a(K) be the number of integer pairs (m, n) with a ≤ m ≤ n and a² + m² + n² + amn ≤ K. Then N_a(K) = log((√(a−2) + √(a+2))/2)·(K − a²)/√(a² − 4) − E_a(K) + O(√K), where E_a(K) = ((K − a²)/a)·(U√(1 + U²) + arsinh U − U²) with U = a²/(2√(K − a²)) accounts for the excluded strip 0 ≤ m < a; E_a(K) ≍ a√K for a ≤ K^{1/4}.
hypotheses: The region is a piece of the interior of a hyperbola-type conic in the (m, n)-plane; the constant in O(√K) is absolute.
proofSteps: The inequality defines an ellipse-like region {m² + n² + amn ≤ K − a²} which for a ≥ 3 is the region between two lines of a hyperbola; restrict to a ≤ m ≤ n.
Count lattice points by columns: for each m the n-range is an interval of explicit length; sum with error O(1) per column and O(√K) columns.
Integrate the column lengths: the full sector gives the log term and the strip 0 ≤ m < a gives E_a(K).
acceptance: a = 3, K large: the main term is log((1 + √5)/2)·(K − 9)/√5.

sources.match: States the count with main term log[(√(a−2)+√(a+2))/2](K − a²)/√(a²−4) + O(√K); the strip correction E_a(K) is missing in the source (PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E1, confirmed).

nodes.title: Counting points in the Markoff fundamental sets
nodes.statement: Let R⁺(K) = #{(x₁, x₂, x₃) ∈ ℤ³ : 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃, x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ ≤ K} and R⁻(K) = #{(x₁, x₂, x₃) ∈ ℤ³ : 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃ ≤ x₁x₂/2, 1 ≤ x₁x₂x₃ − x₁² − x₂² − x₃² ≤ K}. Then R^±(K) = (1/48)K(log K)² + O(K log K).
hypotheses: The constant is 1/48 for both signs (corrected from the printed 1/36 for R⁺).
proofSteps: Sum markoff-fibre-count over 3 ≤ a ≤ K^{1/3} (the condition a ≤ m ≤ n forces a³ ≲ K). The main terms are (1/2)(log a)K/a·(1 + O(1/a)), and Σ_{a≤K^{1/3}}(K/2)(log a)/a = (K/4)(log K^{1/3})² + O(K log K) = K(log K)²/36 + O(K log K).

The strip corrections are O(a√K) for a ≤ K^{1/4} (in total Σ_{a≤K^{1/4}} a√K = O(K)) and (K/a)(log(a²/√K) + O(1)) for K^{1/4} ≤ a ≤ K^{1/3}; with u = log a their sum is K∫_{L/4}^{L/3}(2u − L/2)du + O(K log K) = K(log K)²/144 + O(K log K), L = log K. Hence R⁺(K) = K(log K)²(1/36 − 1/144) = K(log K)²/48 + O(K log K).
R⁻ is treated by the analogous column count for the region 1 ≤ x₁x₂x₃ − Σx_i² ≤ K with x₃ ≤ x₁x₂/2.
acceptance: The two counts have the same main term.

sources.match: States R⁺(K) = (1/36)K(log K)² + O(K log K) and R⁻(K) = (1/48)K(log K)² + O(K log K); the reviewed extraction re-derived 1/48 for both (PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E1, confirmed).

nodes.title: Blomer–Granville bound for pairs of representations
nodes.statement: There is an absolute constant C such that for all K ≥ 2 and integers d ≥ 1, the number of (s₁, s₂, t₁, t₂) ∈ ℤ⁴ with s₁² + d t₂² = s₂² + d t₁², |s_j| ≤ K^{1/2} and |t_j| ≤ (K/d)^{1/2} is at most C·(K/√d + K(log K)τ(d)/d).
hypotheses: τ is the divisor function; the bound is uniform in d.
proofSteps: Rewrite the equation as (s₁ − s₂)(s₁ + s₂) = d(t₁ − t₂)(t₁ + t₂); count the diagonal solutions (s₁ = ±s₂, t₁ = ±t₂) directly and the others by divisor counting in boxes, as in Blomer–Granville.
acceptance: d = 1: the bound K + K log K matches the count of (s, t) pairs with s₁² − s₂² = t₁² − t₂².

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 9.5, p.29, citing Blomer–Granville, Duke Math. J. 135 (2006), Theorem 2
sources.match: Uses the bound ≪ K/√d + K(log K)τ(d)/d for the number of such quadruples with absolute implied constants.

nodes.title: Lattice points on a hyperplane in the positive orthant
nodes.statement: Let d ≥ 2, L = v + Λ ⊆ ℤ^d a translate of a full lattice Λ ⊆ ℤ^d by an integer vector, and a_1, …, a_d positive integers. There are k ≥ 1, s ∈ ℤ/k and r > 0 such that for every integer n ≥ 1, L′(n) = L ∩ {Σ a_i x_i = n} is empty unless n ≡ s mod k, and if n ≡ s mod k then #(L′(n) ∩ ℝ^d_{≥0}) = r·n^{d−1} + O_{d,L,a}(n^{d−2}).
hypotheses: All a_i > 0: with some a_i = 0 the count is infinite (PAPER-LIU-WOOD-ZUREICKBROWN-24/E8, confirmed); then the simplex {x ≥ 0, Σa_ix_i = n} is bounded.
proofSteps: The values Σ a_i x_i on L form a coset s + kℤ of a subgroup kℤ ⊆ ℤ (k = gcd of the a-values on Λ).
For n ≡ s mod k, L′(n) is a translate of the rank-(d − 1) lattice Λ ∩ {Σa_ix_i = 0} inside the hyperplane; the points with x ≥ 0 lie in the dilated simplex n·Δ, Δ = {x ≥ 0, Σa_ix_i = 1}.

Apply the fixed-lattice count with Lipschitz boundary (GlobalNumberFields Layer 3) or semialgebraic-family-lattice-count in the hyperplane: main term vol(nΔ)/det = r n^{d−1} with r = vol(Δ)/covol, error O(n^{d−2}).

sources.match: States the result for non-negative a_i not all zero; positivity is needed for finiteness (E8).

nodes.title: Transference with Minkowski's constant
nodes.statement: Let L be a full lattice in an n-dimensional real inner-product space (n ≥ 1) with polar (inner dual) L*, λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_n the successive minima of L and λ*_1 ≤ … ≤ λ*_n those of L* for the closed unit ball B. Then 1 ≤ λ_iλ*_{n+1−i} ≤ c(n) for every i, with c(n) = 4ⁿ/vol(B)².
hypotheses: Euclidean ball on both sides; the constant is weaker than Banaszczyk's n (dual-transference-upper) but the proof is complete from Minkowski's second theorem.
proofSteps: Lower bound: dual-transference-lower (for every j, λ_jλ*_{n+1−j} ≥ 1).
Minkowski's second theorem for L and L* (GN.1 minkowski-second-upper) with covol(L)covol(L*) = 1 (GN.0 covolume-dual): ∏_j λ_j·∏_j λ*_j ≤ 4ⁿ/vol(B)².
Hence λ_iλ*_{n+1−i} = ∏_j(λ_jλ*_{n+1−j}) / ∏_{j≠i}(λ_jλ*_{n+1−j}) ≤ 4ⁿ/vol(B)², the denominator being ≥ 1.
acceptance: L = ℤⁿ: all minima are 1 and the products equal 1.

sources.locator: §2.4, Theorem 2.20, its remark and proof, printed pp.32–33
sources.match: Proves 1 ≤ λ_iλ*_{n+1−i} ≤ c(n) and notes that Minkowski's second theorem gives c(n) = 4ⁿvol(Bⁿ)^{−2}.

nodes.title: Covering from a lower bound on the dual lattice
nodes.statement: Let L be a full lattice in ℝⁿ (n ≥ 1) with polar L* = {y : ⟨y, x⟩ ∈ ℤ for all x ∈ L}, and R > 0. (a) If ‖y‖₂ ≥ R for every nonzero y ∈ L*, then every b ∈ ℝⁿ has some x ∈ L with ‖x − b‖₂ ≤ n/R. (b) If ‖y‖_∞ ≥ R for every nonzero y ∈ L*, then every b has some x ∈ L with ‖x − b‖_∞ ≤ ‖x − b‖₂ ≤ n/R. In terms of a basis matrix B (L = Bℤⁿ, L* = (Bᵀ)^{−1}ℤⁿ) the constant n depends only on n.
hypotheses: The hypothesis in (b) is weaker than in (a) only up to √n; since ‖y‖₂ ≥ ‖y‖_∞, (b) follows from (a) directly.
proofSteps: (a) μ(L)·λ_1(L*) ≤ n (covering-dual-transference) and λ_1(L*) ≥ R give μ(L) ≤ n/R; the covering radius is attained (covering-radius).
(b) ‖y‖₂ ≥ ‖y‖_∞ ≥ R, so (a) applies; finally ‖x − b‖_∞ ≤ ‖x − b‖₂.
Evertse's Corollary 2.21 gives the same with constant n·c(n)/2 from transference-minkowski-constant, without Gaussian sums.
acceptance: L = ℤⁿ, R = 1: every b is within ‖·‖_∞-distance 1/2 ≤ n of ℤⁿ.
n = 1, L = aℤ, L* = a^{−1}ℤ, R = 1/a: distance a/2 ≤ a.

sources.match: If every nonzero y ∈ L* has ‖y‖₂ > R then every b is within Euclidean distance n·c(n)/(2R) of L.

nodes.title: The minimum of a Construction A lattice
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, n ≥ 1, C ⊆ 𝔽_pⁿ a linear code and L_C = {x ∈ ℤⁿ : x mod p ∈ C} its unscaled Construction A lattice. For c ∈ C let wt_E(c) = Σ_i c̃_i², where c̃_i ∈ ℤ is the representative of c_i with |c̃_i| ≤ p/2 (the Euclidean weight). Then min{‖x‖² : x ∈ L_C ∖ {0}} = min(p², min_{c ∈ C∖{0}} wt_E(c)) (with the second term omitted for C = 0). For p = 2, wt_E is the Hamming weight, so the minimal norm is min(4, d(C)).
hypotheses: The real realisation is the one of construction-a-real-lattice-interface (scale 1); the rescaled lattice p^{−1/2}L_C has minimal norm divided by p.
proofSteps: If x ∈ L_C is nonzero with x ∈ pℤⁿ then ‖x‖² ≥ p², attained by pe_1.
Otherwise c = x mod p ≠ 0 and |x_i| ≥ |c̃_i| coordinatewise, so ‖x‖² ≥ wt_E(c); the lift (c̃_i) itself lies in L_C.
For p = 2, c̃_i ∈ {0, 1} and wt_E(c) = wt_H(c).
acceptance: C = 0: L_C = pℤⁿ and the minimal norm is p².
C = 𝔽_pⁿ: L_C = ℤⁿ and the minimum is 1 = wt_E(e_1).
The extended Hamming [8,4,4] code over 𝔽₂ gives minimal norm min(4, 4) = 4 (the E₈ lattice scaled by √2).

sources.match: For a binary linear code the Construction A lattice has volume 2^{n−k} and squared minimum distance min(4, d_c), d_c the minimum Hamming distance, because 2ℤⁿ is contained in the lattice; the general-p statement with Euclidean weights is proved in the steps by the same comparison.

nodes.title: The space of unimodular lattices
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 let G_n = SL_n(ℝ) with its matrix topology and Γ_n = SL_n(ℤ), embedded in G_n by the entrywise cast. The space of unimodular lattices is X_n = G_n/Γ_n (left cosets gΓ_n) with the quotient topology and its Borel σ-algebra, with the continuous left action h·gΓ_n = hgΓ_n. The map gΓ_n ↦ gℤⁿ (the lattice spanned by the columns of g) is a bijection from X_n onto the set of full lattices in ℝⁿ of covolume 1, equivariant for the linear action of SL_n(ℝ). The right-coset model Γ_n\G_n (lattice spanned by the rows) is identified with X_n by Γ_ng ↦ gᵀΓ_n, a homeomorphism intertwining right multiplication by h with left multiplication by hᵀ.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; X_1 is a point.
Column convention: g ↦ gℤⁿ; consumers in the row convention compose with the transpose homeomorphism.
The topology is the quotient topology; on lattices it is the topology of convergence of bases (Chabauty), which agrees with it.
proofSteps: G_n is a locally compact second countable topological group (closed embedding into matrices, Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.isClosedEmbedding_val) and Γ_n is a discrete subgroup, so X_n is a locally compact Hausdorff space and the quotient map is open.

gℤⁿ = g'ℤⁿ iff g⁻¹g' ∈ GL_n(ℤ), and det g = det g' = 1 forces det(g⁻¹g') = 1, i.e. g⁻¹g' ∈ SL_n(ℤ), so the map is injective; it is surjective onto covolume-one lattices because every such lattice has a basis whose matrix has determinant +1 (change the sign of one basis vector if necessary).
Transpose: Γ_ng ↦ gᵀΓ_n is well defined since (γg)ᵀ = gᵀγᵀ and Γ_n is transpose-stable; it is a homeomorphism as transpose is continuous and involutive, and (gh)ᵀ = hᵀgᵀ gives the intertwining.
acceptance: X_2 is identified with the unit tangent bundle of the modular surface; the point Γ_2 corresponds to ℤ².
diag(t, t^{−1})ℤ² leaves every compact set as t → ∞ (mahler-compactness).

nodes.title: The invariant probability on the space of lattices
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2 there is a unique SL_n(ℝ)-invariant Borel probability measure μ_n on X_n. It is the normalised pushforward of a Haar measure of SL_n(ℝ) along the quotient map: for a fundamental domain F of Γ_n in SL_n(ℝ), μ_n(A) = m_G(F ∩ π⁻¹A)/m_G(F), and m_G(F) < ∞ because Γ_n is a lattice.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2 (for n = 1 the space is a point and μ_1 is the Dirac mass).
Uniqueness is among G-invariant Borel probability measures; there are many invariant infinite measures on other homogeneous spaces, none here.
proofSteps: SL_n(ℝ) is unimodular (no nontrivial continuous homomorphisms to ℝ_{>0}), so a left Haar measure is right invariant and induces a G-invariant measure on G/Γ_n (QuotientMeasureEqMeasurePreimage).
Finite covolume: Siegel sets cover SL_n(ℝ) up to Γ_n and have finite Haar measure (AdelicAlgebraicGroups AA.3, 'S-arithmetic subgroups are lattices' with S = {∞}, or gln-real-reduction); normalise.

Uniqueness: a G-invariant Borel probability on G/Γ_n lifts, through a measurable fundamental domain, to a left-invariant Radon measure on G, i.e. a Haar measure, unique up to the scalar fixed by the total mass.
acceptance: μ_2 corresponds, under X_2 ≅ T¹(SL_2(ℤ)\ℍ), to the normalised Liouville measure; the hyperbolic area of the modular surface is π/3.

nodes.title: Mahler's criterion with the sup norm
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2 and ε > 0 the set {x ∈ X_n : ‖v‖_∞ ≥ ε for every nonzero v ∈ toLattice x} is compact, and a subset of X_n is relatively compact iff the sup-norm first minimum is bounded below on it by a positive constant. The same holds with ‖·‖_∞ replaced by any norm on ℝⁿ.
hypotheses: The equivalence of norms changes ε by a factor depending only on n.
proofSteps: ‖v‖_∞ ≤ ‖v‖₂ ≤ √n‖v‖_∞, so the sup-norm set for ε lies between the Euclidean sets for ε and √n·ε.
Apply the Euclidean criterion (mahler-compactness); closedness of the sup-norm set follows from continuity of the sup-norm first minimum on X_n.
acceptance: For n = 2, the set with ε = 1 contains base (ℤ²) and diag(t, 1/t)·base only for t = 1.

sources.match: Mahler's criterion: a subset of the space of unimodular lattices is relatively compact iff the norms of nonzero vectors are bounded below.

nodes.title: Bounded bases for lattices without short vectors
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 and ε > 0 there is A(n, ε) such that every full lattice L ⊆ ℝⁿ of covolume 1 with λ_1(L) ≥ ε has a ℤ-basis b_1, …, b_n with ‖b_j‖ ≤ A(n, ε) for all j; equivalently L = gℤⁿ with g ∈ SL_n(ℝ) of operator norm ≤ A and ‖g⁻¹‖ ≤ A'(n, ε).
hypotheses: Covolume exactly 1 (bounded covolume suffices with A depending on the bound).
proofSteps: Minkowski's second theorem: λ_1⋯λ_n ≤ 2ⁿ/V_n, so λ_n ≤ 2ⁿ/(V_n ε^{n−1}).
adapted-basis-coordinates (or GN.1 basis-from-minima) gives a basis with ‖b_j‖ ≤ jλ_j ≤ n·λ_n.
The inverse: the rows of g⁻¹ form the dual basis, whose norms are ≤ ∏_{i≠j}‖b_i‖/covol by Cramer and Hadamard.
acceptance: L = ℤⁿ: the standard basis, A = 1.
L = diag(ε, 1/ε)ℤ²: the basis (ε, 0), (0, 1/ε) has norm 1/ε, consistent with A(2, ε) ≥ 1/ε.

sources.match: Mahler's criterion, whose proof reduces to bases bounded in terms of ε.

nodes.title: Diagonal and unipotent flows on the space of lattices
nodes.statement: On X_n the diagonal flow of a vector (s_1, …, s_n) with Σ s_i = 0 is a_t·x = diag(e^{s_1t}, …, e^{s_nt})·x, and the unipotent flow of a nilpotent matrix N is u_t·x = exp(tN)·x (t ∈ ℝ). For n = 2, a_t = diag(e^t, e^{−t}), u_t = [[1, t], [0, 1]] and ū_t = [[1, 0], [t, 1]]; they satisfy a_s u_t a_{−s} = u_{e^{2s}t}. The time-one map of a is T(x) = a_1·x.
hypotheses: Left action on G/Γ (column convention). In the row convention Γ\G the same flows act on the right; the transpose homeomorphism of space-of-unimodular-lattices exchanges u_t with ū_t.
proofSteps: t ↦ a_t and t ↦ u_t are continuous homomorphisms ℝ → SL_n(ℝ) (matrix exponential), so they define continuous flows on X_n preserving μ_n.
The commutation relation is a matrix identity.
acceptance: a_t·base for n = 2 is e^tℤ × e^{−t}ℤ.

sources.locator: §1.1, the geodesic flow γ_t and horocycle flow η_t on Γ\SL(2, ℝ), and Proposition 3.2.3, printed p.102
sources.match: The diagonal and unipotent one-parameter subgroups of SL(2, ℝ) with the relation a^{−s}u^ta^{s} = u^{e^{s}t} used in the Mautner phenomenon (row convention, right action).

nodes.title: The Mautner phenomenon
nodes.statement: Let G be a Lie group, Γ a lattice and μ a probability measure on Γ\G invariant under one-parameter subgroups u_t and a_s with a_{−s}u_ta_s = u_{e^s t}. If f ∈ L²(Γ\G, μ) is essentially a_s-invariant then f is essentially u_t-invariant.
hypotheses: Only the commutation relation and invariance of μ under both flows are used.
proofSteps: The unitary operators U_t, A_s of right translation satisfy A_{−s}U_tA_s = U_{e^s t}.
If A_sf = f then ‖U_tf − f‖ = ‖A_{−s}U_tA_sf − f‖ = ‖U_{e^st}f − f‖ for all s; letting s → −∞ and using strong continuity of t ↦ U_t gives U_tf = f.
acceptance: G = SL(2, ℝ): the geodesic flow and horocycle flow satisfy the relation.

sources.match: States the Mautner phenomenon in this form, with the ergodicity consequences for the geodesic flow.

nodes.title: Mixing of noncompact one-parameter flows
nodes.statement: Let G be a connected simple Lie group with finite centre, Γ a lattice, μ the G-invariant probability measure on Γ\G, and g_t a one-parameter subgroup whose closure is not compact. Then for all φ, ψ ∈ L²(Γ\G, μ): ∫ φ(xg_t)ψ(x) dμ(x) → (∫φ dμ)(∫ψ dμ) as t → ∞. In particular g_t is mixing and ergodic, and so is every time-t₀ map x ↦ xg_{t₀} with t₀ ≠ 0.
hypotheses: The limit is the product of the integrals, not of the L² norms (sourceIssue E402).
G simple (not merely semisimple): for products one must leave every compact set in each factor.
proofSteps: Reduce to φ, ψ in the orthogonal complement ℋ of the constants.

Take a weak limit P of the unitary operators ρ(g_t) along a sequence t_k → ∞; write g_t via the Cartan decomposition and use the Mautner phenomenon (mautner-phenomenon) to show that any vector fixed by P is fixed by the unipotent subgroups U and V attached to g_t.
U and V generate G (G simple), so such a vector is G-invariant, hence 0 in ℋ (μ is G-invariant and ergodic); thus every weak limit is 0, which is the claim.
The time-t₀ statement follows by restricting to t ∈ t₀ℕ.
acceptance: G = SL(2, ℝ), Γ = SL(2, ℤ), g_t = diag(e^{t/2}, e^{−t/2}): the geodesic flow on the modular surface is mixing.
For φ = ψ = 1_A with 0 < μ(A) < 1 the limit is μ(A)², not μ(A).

sources.locator: Remark 3.2.8, Theorem 3.2.9, Remark 3.2.10 and the opening of the proof, printed p.103 (arXiv:math/0310402)
sources.match: States and proves mixing of one-parameter subgroups with noncompact closure on finite-volume quotients of connected simple Lie groups with finite centre; the displayed limit is misprinted as ‖φ‖₂‖ψ‖₂ (E402).

nodes.title: Mixing of the time-one map of the diagonal flow on X_2
nodes.statement: Let T : X_2 → X_2 be x ↦ a_1·x with a_1 = diag(e, e^{−1}). Then T preserves μ_2, is mixing (μ(T^{−k}A ∩ B) → μ(A)μ(B) for all Borel A, B) and hence ergodic.
hypotheses: Left action in the column convention; the row-convention statement for x ↦ x·a_1 on Γ\G follows through the transpose homeomorphism.
proofSteps: Transport to the right quotient by space-of-unimodular-lattices (transposeHomeomorph); there a_1 acts by right multiplication by a_1ᵀ = a_1.
SL(2, ℝ) is connected and simple with centre {±1} and {a_t} has noncompact closure; apply homogeneous-mixing with t ∈ ℕ to indicator functions.
Mixing implies ergodicity (if T⁻¹A = A then μ(A) = μ(A)²).
acceptance: Continuous-flow ergodicity alone would not give ergodicity of T; mixing does.

sources.match: Mixing of one-parameter subgroups with noncompact closure, applied to the geodesic flow on Γ\SL(2, ℝ).

nodes.title: (C, α)-good functions
nodes.statement: Let V ⊆ ℝ^d and C, α > 0. A continuous f : V → ℝ is (C, α)-good on V if for every open ball B ⊆ V and every ε > 0: |{x ∈ B : |f(x)| < ε}| ≤ C·(ε/‖f‖_B)^α·|B|, where ‖f‖_B = sup_B |f| and |·| is Lebesgue measure (with the convention 1/0 = ∞, so the condition is empty when f vanishes on B).
hypotheses: Continuity of f; balls are open Euclidean balls contained in V.
proofSteps: Closure properties: |f| and λf are (C, α)-good when f is; sup_{i∈I}|f_i| is (C, α)-good when every f_i is.
Polynomials: a real polynomial of degree ≤ k in one variable is (2k(k+1)^{1/k}, 1/k)-good on ℝ, by Lagrange interpolation at k + 1 well-separated points where |f| < ε.

sources.match: Defines (C, α)-good functions, proves the closure properties and that polynomials of degree ≤ k are (2k(k+1)^{1/k}, 1/k)-good on ℝ.

nodes.title: Kleinbock–Margulis quantitative nondivergence
nodes.statement: Let d, k ∈ ℕ, C, α > 0, 0 < ρ ≤ 1/k, B = B(x₀, r₀) ⊆ ℝ^d a ball, B̃ = B(x₀, 3^k r₀) and h : B̃ → GL_k(ℝ) continuous. For a primitive subgroup Γ of ℤ^k let ψ_Γ(x) = ‖h(x)Γ‖ (the covolume of h(x)Γ in its span). Suppose that for every Γ: (i) ψ_Γ is (C, α)-good on B̃ and (ii) sup_B ψ_Γ ≥ ρ. Then for every 0 < ε ≤ ρ: |{x ∈ B : δ(h(x)ℤ^k) < ε}| ≤ k·C·(3^d N_d)^k·(ε/ρ)^α·|B|, where δ(Λ) is the length of a shortest nonzero vector and N_d is the Besicovitch constant of ℝ^d.
hypotheses: N_d depends only on d; Γ ranges over all nonzero primitive subgroups of ℤ^k.
proofSteps: Mark points x ∈ B by flags of primitive subgroups Γ with ψ_Γ(x) small relative to ψ_Γ on balls around x (the poset argument of Kleinbock–Margulis §4).
A Besicovitch covering argument and the good property bound the measure of unmarked points; at a marked point x, Minkowski's theorem on the successive quotients of the flag shows δ(h(x)ℤ^k) ≥ ε.
acceptance: k = 1: h(x) is a scalar and the statement is the good property of |h| itself.
Constant h(x) = g: the set is empty or all of B according as δ(gℤ^k) ≥ ε or not, consistent with (ii).

sources.locator: §5, Theorem 5.2 and the opening of its proof, which reduces it to Theorem 4.1 of §4, p.14 (arXiv:math/9810036); §4 not read
sources.match: States the measure bound k C (3^d N_d)^k (ε/ρ)^α |B| under hypotheses (i)–(ii) on the functions ψ_Γ.

nodes.title: Quantitative recurrence of unipotent trajectories
nodes.statement: For every lattice Λ ⊆ ℝ^k there is ρ = ρ(Λ) > 0 such that for every one-parameter unipotent subgroup {u_x} of SL_k(ℝ), every T > 0 and every ε ≤ ρ: |{0 < x < T : δ(u_xΛ) < ε}| ≤ 2k·3^k·(k² + 1)^{1/k²}·(ε/ρ)^{1/k²}·T. Consequently, for every x₀ ∈ X_k and η > 0 there is a compact K ⊆ X_k with |{t ∈ [0, T] : u_t x₀ ∉ K}| ≤ ηT for all T > 0.
hypotheses: ρ depends on Λ (not on u or T); the compact set in the consequence is uniform in T, which strengthens base unipotent-nondivergence.
proofSteps: Write Λ = gℤ^k and h(x) = u_xg. For a primitive Γ with basis v_1, …, v_j the coordinates of h(x)(v_1 ∧ ⋯ ∧ v_j) are polynomials of degree ≤ k² in x, hence (2k²(k² + 1)^{1/k²}, 1/k²)-good (good-functions), and so is ψ_Γ.
ρ = min(1/k, inf_Γ ‖gΓ‖) > 0 by discreteness of Λ; ψ_Γ(0) ≥ ρ gives (ii) on (0, T).
Apply quantitative-nondivergence with d = 1 (N_1 = 2).
The consequence: choose ε with the bound ≤ η and K = {δ ≥ ε}, compact by mahler-compactness-sup-norm (Euclidean version).
acceptance: k = 2, Λ = ℤ², u_x = [[1, x],[0, 1]]: every nonzero vector (p + xq, q) of u_xℤ² has norm ≥ 1 (q ≠ 0 gives |q| ≥ 1, q = 0 gives |p| ≥ 1), so the exceptional set is empty for ε ≤ ρ = 1/2: the periodic horocycle through ℤ² never approaches the cusp.

sources.match: States the bound 2k3^k(k²+1)^{1/k²}(ε/ρ)^{1/k²}T for unipotent trajectories, as a quantitative strengthening of Dani's theorem.
The qualitative recurrence statement for unipotent flows on Γ\G.

nodes.title: Borel's density theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a closed subgroup of SL_ℓ(ℝ) and Γ a lattice in G (discrete with G/Γ of finite G-invariant measure). Then the Zariski closure of Γ in SL_ℓ(ℝ) (the common zero set of all polynomial functions in the matrix entries vanishing on Γ) contains every unipotent element and every hyperbolic (diagonalisable over ℝ with positive eigenvalues) element of G.
hypotheses: G closed in SL_ℓ(ℝ); no connectedness or semisimplicity is assumed in this form.
The conclusion concerns unipotent and hyperbolic elements, not all of G.
proofSteps: Let Γ̄ be the Zariski closure; G acts on the space of polynomials of bounded degree and the line of a polynomial vanishing on Γ̄ gives a finite measure on a projective space invariant under the image of G/Γ.

For a unipotent or hyperbolic g, the iterates g^m push every point of projective space towards a g-fixed point (polynomial or exponential growth); Poincaré recurrence for the finite invariant measure on G/Γ forces g to fix the relevant points, so g ∈ Γ̄.
acceptance: Γ = SL_ℓ(ℤ) in G = SL_ℓ(ℝ): Γ is Zariski dense.
A finite group Γ is a lattice only in a compact G, which has no nontrivial unipotent elements: consistent.

sources.locator: Proposition 4.7.1, printed p.139 (arXiv:math/0310402; statement read, proof not read)
sources.match: States and proves that the Zariski closure of a lattice in a closed subgroup of SL(ℓ, ℝ) contains its unipotent and hyperbolic elements.
Uses Borel density: for a lattice Γ_S in a closed connected S, the real points of the Zariski closure of Γ_S contain the unipotents of S.

nodes.title: Connected subgroups between SO(2,1) and SL(3,ℝ)
nodes.statement: Let H = SO(Q₀)° ⊆ SL_3(ℝ) for Q₀ = x₁² + x₂² − x₃². The only connected Lie subgroups S of SL_3(ℝ) with H ⊆ S are S = H and S = SL_3(ℝ).
hypotheses: Connected subgroups; the statement is about Lie algebras 𝔥 ⊆ 𝔰 ⊆ 𝔰𝔩_3(ℝ).
proofSteps: Under H ≅ PSL_2(ℝ) (or SO(2,1)° ≅ PSL_2(ℝ)), 𝔰𝔩_3(ℝ) = 𝔥 ⊕ 𝔭 with 𝔭 the 5-dimensional irreducible representation (traceless Q₀-symmetric matrices).
An 𝔥-invariant subspace 𝔰 ⊇ 𝔥 is 𝔥 ⊕ (𝔰 ∩ 𝔭), and irreducibility of 𝔭 forces 𝔰 ∩ 𝔭 ∈ {0, 𝔭}.
acceptance: The Lie algebra 𝔰𝔬(2,1) has dimension 3 and 𝔰𝔩_3 dimension 8 = 3 + 5.

sources.locator: §1.2, proof of Margulis' theorem, printed pp.14–15 (arXiv:math/0310402)
sources.match: Uses that a connected subgroup containing H = SO(2,1)° is H or SL(3, ℝ), as part of the proof via Ratner's orbit closure theorem.

nodes.title: Closed SO(Q) orbits come from rational forms
nodes.statement: Let Q = λQ₀∘g with g ∈ SL_3(ℝ), λ ≠ 0, and H = SO(Q₀)°. If the orbit H·gΓ_3 ⊆ X_3 (the lattices hgℤ³, h ∈ H) is closed and carries a finite H-invariant measure, then Q is a scalar multiple of a form with integer coefficients.
hypotheses: Q indefinite nondegenerate ternary; the closed orbit is the alternative left by Ratner's orbit closure theorem with S = H.
proofSteps: Closed finite-volume orbit ⇒ Γ_H = gHg⁻¹ ∩ SL_3(ℤ) is a lattice in gHg⁻¹ = SO(Q)° (Morris §1.1 exercises 22, 24).

Borel density (borel-density): the Zariski closure of Γ_H contains all unipotents of SO(Q)°, which generate it, so SO(Q)° lies in the Zariski closure of a set of integer matrices; that closure is defined over ℚ.

The space of quadratic forms invariant under SO(Q) is the line ℝQ; it is cut out by linear equations with rational coefficients (invariance under the rational generators), so it contains a nonzero rational form.
acceptance: Q = x² + y² − 3z²: the orbit of SO(Q)° is closed (Q rational).

sources.locator: §1.2, proof of Margulis' theorem, printed pp.14–15
sources.match: Shows that if the orbit closure is the H-orbit itself then the orbit is closed with finite volume, H ∩ gΓg⁻¹ is a lattice, and Borel density forces Q to be a multiple of an integral form.

nodes.title: Reduction of Oppenheim's theorem to three variables
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 4 and Q a real nondegenerate indefinite quadratic form in n variables that is not a scalar multiple of a rational form. Then there is a rational 3-dimensional subspace W ⊆ ℚⁿ (with W ⊗ ℝ spanned by integer vectors) such that Q|_{W⊗ℝ} is nondegenerate, indefinite and not a scalar multiple of a rational form; restricting to W ∩ ℤⁿ ≅ ℤ³ gives Q(ℤⁿ) ⊇ Q|_W(ℤ³).
hypotheses: The subspace is rational, so W ∩ ℤⁿ is a lattice of rank 3.
proofSteps: Nondegeneracy, indefiniteness and irrationality are open conditions on the restriction to a 3-dimensional subspace, and the set of rational 3-dimensional subspaces is dense in the Grassmannian.

Irrationality: if every rational 3-dimensional restriction were proportional to a rational form, comparing ratios of coefficients on overlapping subspaces forces all ratios of coefficients of Q to be rational.
acceptance: n = 4, Q = x₁² + x₂² − √2x₃² + x₄²: W = span(e₁, e₂, e₃) works.

sources.locator: §1.2, proof of Margulis' theorem, printed p.14, and Exercise 1.2#15
sources.match: The proof assumes three variables and says the reduction causes no loss of generality, left as Exercise 15.

nodes.title: The Siegel transform
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2 and f : ℝⁿ → [0, ∞] measurable (or f : ℝⁿ → ℂ with Σ|f| finite on every lattice), the Siegel transform of f is the function on X_n given by S f(x) = Σ_{v ∈ toLattice(x) ∖ {0}} f(v), and the primitive Siegel transform is S*f(x) = Σ_{v primitive in toLattice(x)} f(v), where v is primitive in L if v ∉ mL for every integer m ≥ 2. For nonnegative f, S f = Σ_{m≥1} S*(f∘(m·)).
hypotheses: The origin is excluded; for f ≥ 0 the transforms take values in [0, ∞].
Primitivity is in the lattice toLattice(x), not in ℤⁿ.
proofSteps: Well defined on X_n since it depends only on the lattice gℤⁿ.
Every nonzero lattice vector is uniquely m·w with m ≥ 1 and w primitive, giving S f = Σ_m S*(f(m·)).
acceptance: S 1_{B̄(T)} counts the nonzero lattice points in the ball of radius T.
For f compactly supported away from 0 and x in a compact set, S f(x) is a finite sum.

sources.locator: §4, (1), p.10, and the primitive reformulation, pp.11–12
sources.match: Defines E f(g) as the sum of f over the nonzero vectors of the lattice of g, and the equivalent statement with primitive vectors.
Uses f̂(Δ) = Σ_{v∈Δ∖0} f(v) and its primitive version.

nodes.title: Unfolding the primitive Siegel transform
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, G = SL_n(ℝ), Γ = SL_n(ℤ), P ⊆ G the stabiliser of e_n (the mirabolic subgroup) and m_G a Haar measure. For f : ℝⁿ → [0, ∞] measurable: ∫_{G/Γ} S*f dm_{G/Γ} = c·∫_{ℝⁿ} f(x) dx, where c = m_{P/(P∩Γ)}(P/(P∩Γ)) for the compatible Haar measures on P and on G/P ≅ ℝⁿ ∖ {0} (normalised to Lebesgue measure); in particular c < ∞ and does not depend on f.
hypotheses: Tonelli for nonnegative f: no integrability hypothesis.
The constant c is finite because P ∩ Γ ≅ SL_{n−1}(ℤ) ⋉ ℤ^{n−1} is a lattice in P ≅ SL_{n−1}(ℝ) ⋉ ℝ^{n−1}.
proofSteps: Γ acts transitively on primitive vectors of ℤⁿ with stabiliser of e_n equal to P ∩ Γ, so S*f(gΓ) = Σ_{γ ∈ Γ/(P∩Γ)} f(gγe_n).
Unfold: ∫_{G/Γ} Σ_{γ∈Γ/(Γ∩P)} F(gγ) = ∫_{G/(Γ∩P)} F with F(g) = f(ge_n), then integrate over P/(Γ∩P) fibrewise: ∫_{G/P} f(ge_n)·m(P/(Γ∩P)).
G/P ≅ ℝⁿ ∖ {0} via g ↦ ge_n, and the G-invariant measure on it is a multiple of Lebesgue measure (invariant-measures-punctured-space); absorb the multiple into c.
acceptance: n = 2: the stabiliser of e₂ in SL₂(ℤ) is {[[1, 0],[k, 1]] : k ∈ ℤ} and P = {[[1, 0],[t, 1]] : t ∈ ℝ}, so P/(P ∩ Γ) is a circle.

sources.locator: §6 'Lie theoretic formulation of Siegel's integration formula', pp.12–13 (with footnote 4 on the mirabolic subgroup)
sources.match: Rewrites the primitive sum as a sum over Γ/(Γ∩P), unfolds the integral to (Γ∩P)\G and fibres over P\G ≅ ℝⁿ ∖ {0}, so the average is a constant multiple of the Lebesgue integral; the row convention is used there.

nodes.title: Invariant measures on the punctured space
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2, every SL_n(ℝ)-invariant Radon measure on ℝⁿ ∖ {0} is a nonnegative multiple of Lebesgue measure.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2 makes the action transitive; for n = 1 the group is trivial.
proofSteps: SL_n(ℝ) acts transitively on ℝⁿ ∖ {0} with stabiliser P (the mirabolic subgroup), so ℝⁿ ∖ {0} ≅ G/P; Lebesgue measure is G-invariant since det = 1.

An invariant Radon measure on a homogeneous space G/P, when one exists, is unique up to a scalar (it lifts to a Haar measure of G through the quotient integral formula); so every invariant measure is c·Lebesgue.
acceptance: The Dirac mass at e_1 is not invariant; Lebesgue measure restricted to the punctured space is.

sources.match: Siegel's argument: the averaged functional is invariant, hence a multiple of Lebesgue measure on G/P ≅ ℝⁿ ∖ {0}.

nodes.title: Siegel's mean value theorem, primitive form
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2 and f : ℝⁿ → [0, ∞] measurable, ∫_{X_n} S*f dμ_n = (1/ζ(n))·∫_{ℝⁿ} f(x) dx, and ∫_{X_n} S f dμ_n = ∫_{ℝⁿ} f(x) dx. For f ∈ L¹(ℝⁿ), S f is μ_n-integrable and the same identities hold.
hypotheses: μ_n is the invariant probability; the identities hold in [0, ∞] for f ≥ 0 and integrability of S f is a consequence, not a hypothesis.
proofSteps: primitive-siegel-unfolding gives ∫S*f dμ_n = c'·∫f for a constant c' ∈ [0, ∞) independent of f.
S f = Σ_m S*(f(m·)) and ∫f(mx)dx = m^{−n}∫f give ∫S f dμ_n = c'ζ(n)∫f.

Determine c'ζ(n) = 1: for f_T = 1_{B̄(T)}/vol B̄(T), S f_T(x) → 1 as T → ∞ for every x (the lattice toLattice x has covolume 1). Domination: by ball-count-successive-minima S f_T ≤ C·Σ_{j<n} T^{j−n}/(λ_1⋯λ_j) + C for T ≥ 1, and since λ_1⋯λ_n ≍ 1 each 1/(λ_1⋯λ_j) is at most C'·#(toLattice x ∩ B̄(1)) (the vectors realising the minima ≤ 1 generate that many points), which is μ_n-integrable by the first step. Dominated convergence gives c'ζ(n)·1 = 1.
Positive and negative parts give the L¹ statement.
acceptance: n = 2, f = 1_{B̄(T)}: the average number of nonzero lattice points of a random unimodular lattice in a disc of radius T is exactly πT², and of primitive ones πT²/ζ(2) = 6T²/π.

sources.match: Siegel's integration formula: the mean of E f over the space of unimodular lattices equals ∫f; the constant is fixed by a limiting argument or by the Eisenstein-series proof of §15.
States that the proof of Siegel's formula shows the average of the primitive sum is (1/ζ(n))∫f.

nodes.title: The packet of CM points of a negative discriminant
nodes.statement: Let D < 0 be a discriminant (D ≡ 0, 1 mod 4). For a positive definite integral binary form Q = [a, b, c] (a > 0) of discriminant b² − 4ac = D let z_Q = (−b + i√|D|)/(2a) ∈ ℍ, its CM point. z_{Q∘γ} = γ⁻¹·z_Q for γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ), so the classes of primitive forms of discriminant D give a finite set Λ_D of points of the modular curve SL₂(ℤ)\ℍ, of cardinality h(D), the number of proper classes; each point carries the weight 1/ω_Q, ω_Q the order of the stabiliser of z_Q in PSL₂(ℤ) (ω = 3, 2, 1 for D = −3, −4, D < −4). The normalised counting measure of the packet is ν_D = (Σ_Q 1/ω_Q)^{−1}Σ_Q ω_Q^{−1}δ_{z_Q}.
hypotheses: Primitive forms (gcd(a, b, c) = 1); for fundamental D every form of discriminant D is primitive.
Reduced representatives (|b| ≤ a ≤ c) give the points of Λ_D in the standard fundamental domain.
proofSteps: z_Q is the root in ℍ of Q(z, 1) = 0; the transformation law follows from Q(γ(x, y)) and the action of γ on the root.

Proper equivalence classes of forms correspond to SL₂(ℤ)-orbits of CM points of discriminant D; there are h(D) of them (finiteness of the form class number, TauCetiRoadmap IntegralLattices binary forms).
The stabiliser of z_Q in PSL₂(ℤ) is the image of the automorph group of Q, of order 3, 2 or 1.
acceptance: D = −4: Λ_D = {i} with ω = 2.
D = −20: h = 2; the reduced forms [1, 0, 5] and [2, 2, 3] give i√5 and (−1 + i√5)/2.

sources.match: Associates to each ideal class of a negative fundamental discriminant a CM point z_A ∈ F and weights 1/ω_D with ω_D = 3, 2, 1 for D = −3, −4, D < −4.
Defines the h(d) Heegner points z_Q = (−b + √d)/(2a) of a negative discriminant in the fundamental region.

uses.how: equidistribution of Λ_D as D → −∞ through fundamental discriminants
genus version of the CM equidistribution

nodes.title: The oriented closed geodesic of an indefinite form
nodes.statement: Let D > 0 be a nonsquare discriminant and Q = [a, b, c] a primitive integral form of discriminant D. Its roots w = (−b + √D)/(2a) and w' = (−b − √D)/(2a) are the endpoints of the hyperbolic geodesic S_Q = {z ∈ ℍ : a|z|² + b Re z + c = 0}. Let γ_Q ∈ SL₂(ℤ) be the generator of the automorph group of Q with attracting fixed point w (pell-automorph). The oriented closed geodesic C_Q is the image in SL₂(ℤ)\ℍ of the arc of S_Q from z to γ_Qz, oriented from w' towards w; for a continuous SL₂(ℤ)-invariant function f, ∫_{C_Q} f ds is the integral along that arc (hyperbolic arclength), and for an invariant 1-form ω, ∫_{C_Q} ω the integral along the oriented arc. Both are independent of z ∈ S_Q and depend only on the proper class of Q; C_{nQ} = C_Q for n ∈ ℤ_{>0}.
hypotheses: Nonsquare D, so the roots are irrational and γ_Q is hyperbolic.
Orientation from w' to w, i.e. clockwise on S_Q when a > 0.
proofSteps: γ_Q fixes w and w' and preserves S_Q; it acts on S_Q as a translation towards its attracting fixed point w.
Changing z along S_Q changes the arc by a fundamental-domain shift of γ_Q, leaving integrals of invariant integrands unchanged; replacing Q by Q∘γ moves S_Q by γ⁻¹ and conjugates γ_Q.
acceptance: Q = [1, 0, −2] (D = 8): S_Q is the semicircle |z| = √2 and γ_Q = ±[[3, 4],[2, 3]] (t = 6, u = 2 with t² − 8u² = 4).

nodes.title: The length of a closed geodesic
nodes.statement: Let D > 0 be a nonsquare discriminant, Q primitive of discriminant D and (t, u) the solution of t² − Du² = 4 with t, u ≥ 1 minimal. Then the hyperbolic length of C_Q (the arc from z to γ_Qz) is 2 log ε_D with ε_D = (t + u√D)/2, independent of Q. The length is the translation length of the parametrised cycle; it is not halved when C_Q retraces itself (reciprocal classes).
hypotheses: Lengths are for the parametrised arc, counted with multiplicity.
proofSteps: γ_Q = ±[[(t − bu)/2, −cu], [au, (t + bu)/2]] has trace t (pell-automorph).
A hyperbolic element of trace t > 2 translates its axis by 2 arccosh(t/2) = 2 log((t + √(t² − 4))/2) = 2 log ε_D.

sources.match: length(C_A) = 2 log ε_D, with γ_Q the automorph built from the minimal solution of t² − d₀u² = 4 and ε_D = (t + u√D)/2.

nodes.title: Reversing the orientation of a closed geodesic
nodes.statement: For Q = [a, b, c] primitive of nonsquare discriminant D > 0, the geodesic of −Q = [−a, −b, −c] is S_Q traversed in the opposite direction: C_{−Q} has the same image as C_Q, ∫_{C_{−Q}} f ds = ∫_{C_Q} f ds for invariant functions and ∫_{C_{−Q}} ω = −∫_{C_Q} ω for invariant 1-forms. The reflected form [a, −b, c] has geodesic −S̄_Q (the mirror image in the imaginary axis).
hypotheses: The statement is about forms; the narrow-class translation (−Q represents JA⁻¹ when Q represents A) belongs to the class-group dictionary (IntegralLattices binary forms, MultiquadraticPartII).
proofSteps: −Q has the same zero set, so S_{−Q} = S_Q; its attracting fixed point is w' since γ_{−Q} = γ_Q⁻¹ (the formula of pell-automorph with (a, b, c) ↦ (−a, −b, −c)).
Reflection z ↦ −z̄ maps the zero set of [a, b, c] to that of [a, −b, c].
acceptance: Q = [1, 0, −2]: C_{−Q} runs along |z| = √2 counterclockwise.

nodes.title: Weyl sums of spherical harmonics over lattice points on spheres
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 let R_n = {m ∈ ℤ³ : |m|² = n} and r₃(n) = #R_n. For a harmonic polynomial u on ℝ³, homogeneous of degree ℓ, and n with r₃(n) > 0, the Weyl sum is W_u(n) = r₃(n)^{−1}Σ_{m∈R_n} u(m/√n). The theta series with harmonic coefficients is θ(z; u) = Σ_{m∈ℤ³} u(m)e^{2πiz|m|²}, z ∈ ℍ, whose n-th coefficient is a(n) = Σ_{m∈R_n}u(m) = n^{ℓ/2}r₃(n)W_u(n).
hypotheses: u harmonic (Δu = 0) and homogeneous; ℓ = 0 gives W_1(n) = 1.
proofSteps: W_u(n) is the integral of u against the normalised counting measure of R_n/√n ⊆ S².
Homogeneity gives u(m) = n^{ℓ/2}u(m/√n) for m ∈ R_n, hence the coefficient identity.

θ(z; u) converges absolutely on ℍ (polynomial growth against Gaussian decay); its modularity of weight 3/2 + ℓ on Γ₀(4) is the theta input recorded in the base packet's tier-move gap (MetaplecticAutomorphicForms MP.7).
acceptance: u = x: W_u(n) = 0 for every n by the symmetry m ↦ −m.
u = x² − y²: W_u(n) = 0 by the symmetry swapping coordinates.

sources.match: Defines V_n = {m/|m| : |m|² = n}, the Weyl sums W_u(n) and the theta function θ(z; u) with coefficients a(n) = n^{ℓ/2}r₃(n)W_u(n).

nodes.title: Weyl's criterion on the sphere
nodes.statement: Let σ be the normalised rotation-invariant measure on S² and (V_k) a sequence of nonempty finite multisets in S² with counting probability measures ν_k. Then ν_k → σ weakly iff for every ℓ ≥ 1 and every harmonic polynomial u homogeneous of degree ℓ, ν_k(u) → 0.
hypotheses: Weak convergence against continuous functions on S².
proofSteps: Restrictions to S² of harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degrees 0..L span the restrictions of all polynomials of degree ≤ L (harmonic decomposition p = h_L + |x|²p'), so their span is a subalgebra-generated dense subspace of C(S²) by Stone–Weierstrass.
For ℓ ≥ 1, σ(u) = 0 (u is orthogonal to constants; equivalently the mean value property at 0 for harmonic u).
Hence ν_k(f) → σ(f) for f in a dense subspace, and uniform boundedness of the ν_k extends this to C(S²).
acceptance: For n = 3·4^j the set R_n/√n consists of the 8 points (±1, ±1, ±1)/√3, and for the harmonic u = Σx_i⁴ − 3Σ_{i<j}x_i²x_j² one gets W_u(n) = −2/3 for every j: these n are not square-free and are excluded from Duke's theorem.

sources.match: Deduces the uniform distribution of V_n on S² from the bound on W_u(n) 'by the analogue of Weyl's criterion'.

requests.need: Haar measure on SL_n(ℝ) for the real points of SL_n over ℚ, its unimodularity, and the quotient measure on SL_n(ℝ)/SL_n(ℤ) with the quotient integral formula.

SL_n(ℤ) is a lattice in SL_n(ℝ) (the S-arithmetic lattice theorem with S = {∞}, or real reduction by Siegel sets of finite Haar measure), and the analogous statement for the mirabolic P ∩ SL_n(ℤ) in P.
IsLipschitzParametrizable (milestone 3A): finitely many Lipschitz maps from [0,1]^d cover the set, with its closure properties; the fixed-lattice count with error O(c^{n−1}).
Closed subgroups of SL_n(ℝ) are Lie groups with Lie algebras; connected Lie subgroups correspond to Lie subalgebras; the adjoint representation.

All are above GN's tier 3 in the Caraiani–Newton order, so GN.4 cannot cite them; moving them down would re-plan whole roadmaps.

upstreamNotes.note: Layer 3A's lattice-point count is for a fixed lattice (its constant depends on D and Λ). Consumers in counting problems need Widmer's lattice-uniform version with the successive-minima error; the atlas plans it in GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.4 (widmer-lipschitz-count) on top of 3A's IsLipschitzParametrizable.

Layer 6 states CAD and quantifier elimination but not the fibrewise consequence that a semialgebraic family has a uniform bound on the number of cells (hence connected components) of its fibres; GN.4 states it (semialgebraic-uniform-components) for Davenport-type counting. It may sit better in RealAlgebraicGeometry as a corollary of its CAD layer.
